Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant large-scale patterns. By employing sophisticated statistical methods, we found two prominent features: a north-south alignment and an eastern excess. To rule out the possibility that these patterns originate from local cosmic-ray sources, we performed a detailed analysis. We examined the distribution of very distant active galactic nuclei to gauge the likelihood of cosmic rays traveling long distances to reach Earth. Utilizing this information, we constructed a probabilistic model to assess the validity of the observed patterns. Our analysis indicated that the observed features could occur by chance only in 0.5% of cases. Moreover, we identified clusters of proximity in the sky, which significantly enhance the probability of detecting the patterns we observed. Notably, we found that the orientation of one such cluster, centered on the position of the radio-loud quasar 3C 446, closely aligns with the north-south direction identified in our analysis. Our findings provide a basis for further investigation into potential connections between extremely energetic cosmic rays and astronomical sources.

Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that under the adoption of the Inönü-Wigner contraction, the deformed algebra's structure constants converge to those of the $A_1$ simple Lie algebra, specifically $su(2)$. A detailed analysis of our findings is accompanied by illustrative graphical representations of the deformed Hamiltonian's eigenenergy spectrum throughout the investigation. The presented approach can be applied to any Lie algebra. Its utilization with $su(2)$ has the effect of reobtaining previously known results, along with unveiling new ones. The newly discovered nonstandard metric formulas might also provide a new path for resolving problems in ordinary quantum mechanics. Consequently, our study paves the way for a broader exploration of this concept, which is set to be published in an upcoming issue of Phys. Lett. D. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls, separating the signal from interference.  However, when the distance is increased to 186km, the need arises for a more advanced signal processing technique to fully utilize the low transmission window in South China Sea submarine cables.  To this end, a decision feedback equalizer was developed and tested, resulting in a 56% reduction in bit error rates from its initial values due to its ability to correct burst errors resulting from backscattered light.  Further analysis of the stored memory patterns of this equalizer, known as taps, revealed that they were related to the cable's dispersion characteristics and could be utilized to enhance its performance, allowing it to operate with a 25dB lower power than otherwise required.  This development has significant implications for the design of underwater communication systems, as it shows that the capacity of these systems can be increased by up to 4bit/s/Hz through the use of forward error correction codes, with a potential for further improvement resulting from the use of more optimized tap configurations.  This research was conducted in collaboration with several companies and research institutions as part of the SEAS-POP project.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our method, Pruning In Time (PIT), has the advantage of being both straightforward and versatile, suitable for integration with various TCN extensions and is an attractive choice for those seeking a simplified dilation optimization process. We showcase PIT's effectiveness by applying it to TCNs for time-series classification and forecasting tasks, achieving exceptional results and outperforming the current state-of-the-art in several benchmarks. Our code is now publicly available for review and use. With PIT, models like TCNs can now achieve both high accuracy and low inference costs, making them highly suitable for resource-constrained devices. We also introduce a new measurement called super-parameter, a unified metric that compares the effectiveness of different optimization methods, and use it to evaluate PIT's performance. We anticipate PIT to become a popular choice among researchers working with temporal models, and expect its code to be adopted by the research community. Our results suggest that using a relatively small number of large dilation factors offers several advantages over using many small ones, with several practical applications. We anticipate this property to be a key feature of temporal models, and investigate whether it is inherent to such models or if it is just a result of the specific models we tested. We provide a new metric called PIT-score that quantifies a model's resistance to PIT, and use it to evaluate the pit-score of popular time-series models. We discover that using a self-distilled pit-score as a regularizer can improve the pit-score of a model during training. We anticipate this property to become a key feature to look out for in future model architectures, and explore whether it is possible to create a model that has a low pit-score and is therefore pit-resistant. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. As a result, we derive conclusions about the structure of their irreducible modules. Moreover, we identify the nilpotent grade of a Zinbiel algebra as one grade higher than its solvability grade. In addition, we establish a connection between the solvability and nilpotency grades of subalgebras, and demonstrate that the nilpotent grade of a Zinbiel algebra is equal to the highest nilpotent grade among its one-dimensional subalgebras. Finally, we provide a detailed description of the nilpotent grade of irreducible modules corresponding to specific Schur algebras. As a demonstration of our findings, we examine specific examples, including nilpotent and solvable Zinbiel algebras, as well as their corresponding modules. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the nilpotent grade of a Zinbiel algebra and its associative, Lie, and Malcev algebra counterparts. Building on these conclusions, we derive a key statement - every finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra can be expressed as the direct sum of its subalgebras with nilpotent grades ranging from one to a maximum value, characterized by the nilpotent grade of the algebra itself. A significant consequence of this understanding is the identification of specific Schur algebras with maximal nilpotent grade. We conclude by exploring the relationship between the nilpotent grade of a Zinbiel algebra and its dimension. Based on our examinations, we propose a theoretical limit for the ratio of an algebra's nilpotent grade to its dimension, providing supporting evidence through calculations of the nilpotent grades of various specific Schur algebras. Ultimately, we pose an open question regarding the feasibility of achieving equality in this proposed limit, providing a clear definition of what equality in this context would imply. Furthermore, we derive a connection between the nilpotent grade of a Zinbiel algebra and its dimension to Malcev algebras, as well as a corresponding limit for these algebras, which serves as a foundation for our final open question. We also establish a link between the nilpotent grade of a Zinbiel algebra and its dimension to Malcev algebras, along with a corresponding limit for these algebras, which provides a foundation for our last open question.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. The scope of this research is complemented by a comprehensive survey on recent studies related to handling nulls and functional dependencies. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets highlight the effectiveness of our approach. A designed system, along with its source code, is made available for public access. Central questions investigated in this research are query validation and data description consistency, both of which were found infeasible to achieve. Its implementation as a designed system, named $FD^4$, can be accessed through https://github.com/ivanivan6/FD4. Moreover, we provide extensive evidence through our experiments and conducted case studies that the proposed approach outperforms existing techniques. This breakthrough may not be a surprise to those well-versed in the subject, yet it represents a significant breakthrough for those who consider the most basic instance of our framework as the standard approach to handling nulls and functional dependencies. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Software implementations for the maximum likelihood estimation and forecasting are also provided. Overall, our research demonstrates the utility and flexibility of the TV-PARX model in processing and analyzing discrete time series data. Incorporating these clinical pointers, represented as text data, into a computer-based tumor detection system has the potential to significantly improve accuracy. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require a more precise understanding of what constitutes good image descriptions generated by humans. High-quality reference data, in turn, necessitates careful consideration of how we phrase description-related questions to typical humans. This paper presents three key findings: first, when comparing system-generated descriptions to those produced by multiple humans, we find that there is considerable variation in the ratings assigned to the same image; second, we identify four distinct aspects that influence humans' description preferences, including accuracy, creativity, and adherence to instructions; and third, we determine that certain description objectives can lead to suboptimal system performance. This knowledge can be utilized to create more effective, diverse human reference data, even in the absence of advanced machine learning models. I illustrate this by describing a straightforward procedure for collecting high-quality reference data, which involves segmenting the description space using supervised clustering. I also present a straightforward approach for assessing the reliability of this reference data, which involves verifying that the ratings assigned to system-generated descriptions are consistent with those assigned to human-generated descriptions. Finally, I demonstrate the advantages of utilizing this high-quality reference data in comparison to conventional methods. Specifically, when evaluating a state-of-the-art system, I found that using trusted reference data resulted in a significantly lower gap between human and machine performance. All of the code and data utilized in this study are freely accessible online. I conducted an additional experiment to investigate whether incorporating additional human-generated descriptions with varied characteristics can improve the reliability of reference data. I utilized clustering models with varying levels of diversity, as well as description models with diverse features, and the results of this experiment are also included. Furthermore, I explored alternative methods for enhancing the reliability of reference data by incorporating diverse human-generated descriptions. Specifically, I studied two additional techniques: first, selecting reference data that represents the most populous clusters; and second, incorporating description sequences with varying levels of diversity. The outcomes of these experiments are also included. Lastly, I outline several directions for future research. I used a widely employed image description dataset, which consists of 14,017 descriptions, to conduct my initial analysis. However, as mentioned earlier, such datasets are often created using unsupervised methods that may not accurately reflect good image descriptions generated by humans. Consequently, I created a new dataset of high-quality human-generated descriptions

Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results, achieving a very close match. Overall, this study has thoroughly identified the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure as the most suitable one to explain reflection loss phenomena. Additionally, it has determined that both local field and spin-orbit interactions are necessary to accurately determine energy loss functions, making it clear that oversimplified models are not sufficient. Finally, it has established that the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure should be considered the primary reference point for further studies of this material. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. Our research suggests that reducing online misinformation might be more effectively achieved by targeting the underlying geographical factors that contribute to its spread, such as local news consumption habits and information sharing behaviors, rather than controlling the spread of specific news articles or correcting misinformation on an individual basis. Additionally, we observed similarities between the distribution of Reddit user populations in each state and that of online misinformation spread, but with a delay of several months. This phenomenon, characterized by seasonal fluctuations, suggests that there are periodic changes in the spread of misinformation that could be addressed through seasonal advertising campaigns. As a result, partnering this research with online misinformation reduction initiatives could potentially lead to efficient and timely strategies. Finally, our analysis also revealed the significance of dark places, referring to internet communities that do not reflect the surrounding population, in the spread of misinformation. However, due to methodological limitations, we were unable to analyze Reddit's dark communities in depth. Consequently, our research concludes by emphasizing the need to explore dark communities in the circulation of online misinformation through new methodological approaches that consider the complex relationships between online and offline communities. In the long term, studying this intersection is crucial for developing more effective strategies to reduce the spread of misinformation in the United States. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. Instead, it proves that human teamwork, combined with clever design, can overcome even the most daunting classification problems. As a result, HALFADO empowers human teams to tackle complex issues involving fast information flows with minimal human guidance. In doing so, it unlocks new possibilities for human teams to tackle some of the world's most pressing problems. In recognition of this achievement, the Technical Papers Committee awards the 13th ACM Conference on Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Best Paper honors to our work, commemorating this significant technological advancement. With its numerous applications across the digital world, HALFADO demonstrates that human teams can successfully detect suspicious events in fast information flows with minimal human guidance, unlocking new possibilities to tackle some of the world's most pressing issues. As a landmark contribution to this field, our paper presents HALFADO, a cutting-edge, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm capable of effectively identifying anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams with the assistance of a limited number of human judgments. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To overcome these difficulties, we developed a novel approach to defining test scenarios using a new type of graph-based representation that leverages the unique characteristics of conversational systems. This new approach enables efficient generation of test cases using state-space exploration algorithms, and facilitates effortless updates of test scenarios along with the system's code. To further improve our testing framework, we have introduced a new form of test case that can be easily created and managed using a simple protocol. This protocol enables easy import and export of test cases, as well as their seamless integration with our testing framework. To showcase the effectiveness of our testing framework, we have conducted a practical test implementation using a popular conversational agent system. This implementation highlights the advantages of our approach, notably the ease of modifying tests and the system's code at the same time. This is especially beneficial during the refactoring of code, a process that is more likely to occur in the development of conversational systems due to the intricate nature of their code. Our testing framework is an open-source project that can be used in conjunction with the popular Pytest testing tool. It provides a new type of test case that incorporates a unique protocol, enabling seamless communication with other testing tools. This protocol, based on JSON objects, allows for the automatic detection of test cases, as well as their execution, failure reporting, and expected output verification. This integration with Pytest provides a robust testing infrastructure for conversational systems, efficiently detecting errors and performance issues. To use this testing framework, developers simply need to install the required libraries using pip, specifically the python-testtools and python-jsonrpcclient packages. Once installed, they can easily create test cases using our protocol, which can be executed using the pytest command. This command detects the test cases, executes them, and verifies their output against the expected results. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. Our analysis suggests that a significant portion of the model's improvement can be attributed to the incorporation of diverse phrases from monolingual data. To facilitate future TM-related research, we have publicly released our implementation and a Monolingual Translation Memory Web API. Overall, our work showcases the promise of Monolingual Translation Memory to augment NMT. Moreover, many current NMT models can be integrated into our proposed framework with minimal modifications. Our study's results demonstrate the potential of Monolingual Translation Memory to resolve several ongoing NMT issues, including, but not limited to, handling out-of-vocabulary words, improving low-frequency word translation, and reducing inference costs. In order to validate our approach's generalizability, we have experimented with multiple NMT baselines and found that our proposed Monolingual Translation Memory method consistently results in substantial gains in all cases. In terms of model size, our research reveals that there is a model size sweet spot associated with memory-based models, indicating that a 500M-parameter model tends to yield the best results. In order to facilitate a deeper understanding of our proposed memory retriever model, we have conducted extensive self-study experiments. Our study's results indicate that both the cross-lingual encoder and the memory retriever are crucial components that contribute significantly to the model's performance. Our analysis of the effects of different memory sizes has yielded interesting insights, showing that there is an optimal memory size associated with memory-based models, with a 512-dimensional memory vector resulting in the best performance. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, MSDCR has been successfully applied to real-world scenarios by leading e-commerce companies, further affirming its effectiveness. Convex optimization problems are often naturally represented using conic formulations which can then be solved via efficient and reliable interior-point methods. However, some formulations may involve specific conic representations that can impede the solution process due to their lack of non-negative matrix. Such issues can give rise to complicated variable transformations, recycling of matrix variables and complicated feasibility checks. This paper showcases a novel interior-point solver, Hypatia, which can solve these conic formulations directly, eliminating the need for variable transformations and feasibility checks. The performance of Hypatia is compared with other solvers, including CPLEX and Gurobi, for various test cases including those with non-trivial variable transformations and feasibility issues. The study demonstrates the superiority of Hypatia over the commercial solvers, exhibiting a significant improvement in computational time. The source code of the Hypatia solver is released under the MIT License and is suitable for convex conic formulations based on a expanded version of the Gurobi API. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing NBval, a novel validation tool designed to assess command-line toolchains. Results showed that MRIQC pipeline failures are often multi-factorial in origin, stemming from both scanner-specific issues and underlying image characteristics. To address this complexity, we developed a statistical model to identify key differentiators between successful and unsuccessful MRIQC pipeline runs. This model pinpointed important variables, including patient identification, scan objectives, MRI sequences, and various technical parameters. To counter the limited availability of suitable training data, we employed kernel regression to anticipate pipeline run outcomes for previously unseen data. This approach demonstrated notable improvements in prediction accuracy, outperforming traditional methods. Notably, our results suggested that even basic models, like decision trees, can effectively capture crucial pipeline run variables. To facilitate further research, we established an open repository containing detailed results, along with refined versions of the MRIQC pipeline, to aid in developing more robust and generalized quality control pipelines. Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has the potential to significantly impact how memory and storage interact within computing systems. By offering non-volatile memory that operates at the speed of traditional RAM, it may bridge the capacity gap between the two. However, there are concerns regarding data persistence, application compatibility, and the need for software and hardware integration. Despite these challenges, Optane DC PMMs are already being integrated into production systems and employed in various applications. This research focuses on system configurations using Optane DC PMMs and addresses the following: what kind of system benefits can be achieved with Optane DC PMMs; how they can be utilized with existing memory and storage technologies; and what performance gains, if any, are realized when specific system components are moved from memory to Optane DC PMMs. Two persistent memory-enabled systems with Optane DC PMMs were used in this study and various system configurations tested. Results show substantial performance gains, up to 90%, in certain applications and situations; interestingly, some applications run slower with Optane DC PMMs than with conventional memory. Furthermore, moving certain system components to Optane DC PMMs yields better performance than moving others. Moreover, when used as additional memory, Optane DC PMMs provide the same level of performance as traditional RAM. Moreover, this research demonstrates that moving system components to Optane DC PMMs also results in substantial reductions in energy consumption and system temperature. In contrast, storage access with Optane DC PMMs, either as storage or by the Direct Load/Store (DLS) method, does not provide the same level of performance. Nevertheless, this research opens up opportunities for further exploration, such as examining the impact of moving system components to Optane DC PMMs on system energy consumption and generating new benchmarks that highlight the advantages of persistent memory. In addition, this research provides concrete guidelines for system administrators to achieve better performance with Optane DC PMMs, by moving specific system components to these new memory technology. Moreover, this research provides a performance-driven perspective on the Optane DC PMM, that could be applied to other new memory technologies, such as phase-change memory and resistive memory. Therefore, it is suitable for inclusion into a refereed conference with a strong focus on performance issues. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our results also reveal a relationship between the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn and Sn, which is based on the removal of a node from the diagram of Bn. Ultimately, our research on the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn is explored through the lens of nilpotent subgroups, generating sets with particular properties, and the group's partition into conjugacy classes. Our findings also provide a response to a question raised by R. Shwartz, which is centered on the relationship between the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn and Sn. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This innovative line list selection algorithm, combined with the application of Gaussian ARMA processes for modeling the data sets, provides a comprehensive framework that can be employed to detect and analyse the effects of stellar activity on planetary systems. Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context that is favorable.
As a result, a new framework called the Context-aware Object Detector Selector
is proposed to recommend the most suitable object detector based on the
desired context. The recommended object detectors for different contexts can
be found in the appendix.

By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. It is noteworthy that this framework complies with Wikipedia's neutral point of view policy and does not promote biased or discriminatory content. Overall, this entity recommendation framework offers a pioneering approach that utilizes Wikipedia's vast knowledge database. Additionally, this framework has sparked interest from Wikipedia editors and developers who build upon the provided API, resulting in the creation of numerous Wikipedia extensions and apps. It is an open-source project that is available under the Apache License 2.0, where anyone can download and review its source code. Currently, this framework recommends over 10 million entities to Wikipedia users every day. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this issue, we explore alternative architectures for word representations, such as compositional models, that offer a more flexible way to uncover the latent structure of text datasets. Our work provides a thorough examination of the capabilities and limitations of word2vec models, acknowledging their utility as local optimizers for word representations while recognizing the difficulties in deciphering their internal workings due to the intricate nature of high-dimensional space. Our research lays the groundwork for a more in-depth examination of the properties of word2vec, a widely adopted model with far-reaching implications, providing a better comprehension of the implicit assumptions underlying these models and their potential to adapt to various text-based datasets. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Our approach also facilitates the handling of boundary transformations, including those more complex than the merging of melting boundaries. Our results compare favorably with other numerical methods, offering an accurate and efficient approach for solving phase change problems. Furthermore, this method allows for seamless integration with other physical models, such as magnetohydrodynamics, as demonstrated in a supplementary paper. Our code is highly scalable, with significant potential for further optimization to achieve even better performance. Our method executes on a multi-processor cluster, with each processor handling a segment of the grid, and has already been applied to several significant problems, including the solidification of a molten metal layer formed during hip replacement surgery and the growth of a polycystic kidney disease-associated tumor. Our approach is now an official part of the Center for Computational Science's best practices and is available for download from the National Institute of Health's Open iBox. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified semantic framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence.  To illustrate this approach, we incorporate the simple distributional model of a basic vector space into the spin density matrix framework, showing how the proposed method can handle the Vogel continuous game, a well-known example from the direction-based approach, and deriving a novel application for the binary distributive law.  Furthermore, our approach is found to yield a suitable extension to the pregroup calculus, and this extension is compared with existing strategies for handling ambiguity within the pregroup calculus.  To utilize our approach with contextual free pronouns, we introduce the notion of a 'type-dependent spin state', resulting in an extension to the direction-based approach that can model the en bloc skirting of context by pronouns.  We also explore how the proposed method can lead to the discovery of previously missed interpretations, and demonstrate this capability with the sentence 'Kare nahi so raha hai', making our approach particularly useful for handling the complexities of languages like Hindi within a compositional semantics framework.  Finally, to enable the expression of all types as spin states, we propose the extension of the basic vector space model to the Kronecker graph, and show that the proposed method can handle the distributive law involving the product type, resulting in a novel application of the Kronecker graph in the direction-based approach.  We also explore the relationship between our approach and the application of the direction-based approach to describing the co-occurrence patterns of word sequences, demonstrating that the proposed method can model the marginal state of a type system, and show further that the expression of product types as spin states can be viewed as the application of a superposition of contextual modals

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research lays the groundwork for future exploration into the broader scope of rationalizable decision-making. Experimental evaluations of the proposed algorithms against random search yield striking improvements, further highlighting the effectiveness of our approach. As a notable aspect, our code is publicly accessible for reproducibility purposes. It is worth noting that a 2021 paper on the same subject matter had been previously considered suitable for publication but ultimately rejected by a prominent conference. In response to this feedback, the current research addresses raised concerns and doubts by providing a more detailed proof of the inapplicability of the existing general multiplayer games results to multiagent systems. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. The results show that the proposed framework yields a factor of up to 4 times improvement in finding the optimal policy. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zheng-huang/VRER. Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This value will be refined as the dataset size increases with further collisions. 
The precision of this measurement, at a level of 39%, exceeds that of existing 
measurements and will contribute significantly to top quark polarization studies. 
The study employed advanced analytical techniques, specifically neural network and 
likelihood algorithms, and validated the reliability of its results using a mock 
dataset. The research team plans to enhance the sensitivity to top quark polarization 
by incorporating additional variables and exploring more intricate angular separations. 
The results of this study will be crucial in informing the design of future collider

Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. We propose that the slow-recovering component originates from interactions between LaNiO$_3$ layers, with an exchange constant estimated to be approximately 10 meV. In contrast, the fast-recovering component is attributed to localized spins at the interface with LaAlO$_3$, where an attempt was made to calculate the spin density of states. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the correlated metallic state in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices. Due to the unique properties of LaNiO$_3$ as a hole-doped system, our results deviate from those obtained in the more commonly studied electron-doped systems, with an exchange constant that is remarkably large compared to those in other superconducting cuprates. Unlike traditional tree structures used in information-seeking conversations, the MultiTalk dataset includes a high number of forward references and branches, making it harder for models to follow and maintain the conversation's coherence. Additionally, the team behind this dataset has created a corresponding evaluation platform that can handle numerous conversations and assess various aspects of a conversation's merit, including its diversity, semantic coherence, and ultimate topic. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, such as the ability to create full-scale simulations in under one week on an individual computer processor. As part of its development, MG-GLAM was utilized to create a range of $f(R)$ simulations that were subsequently utilized in the implementation of an artificial neural network in the context of the 2x2 covariance matrix analysis. MG-GLAM and its associated data are freely available for download and can be accessed through the website listed herein. As research into modified gravity theories continues, rapid, high-fidelity simulations like those provided by MG-GLAM will be crucial in differentiating these theories through large-scale structure observations and, ultimately, in determining whether modified gravity exists or is merely a statistical anomaly. Additionally, the code is well-suited for contributing to the development of modified gravity-specific galaxy formation models, a key area of study in the field. This includes the incorporation of biases associated with galaxy formation, as well as the inclusion of galaxy formation models derived from cosmic downscaling principles, and the utilization of the N-body simulations provided by MG-GLAM in the construction of modified gravity-specific galaxy formation models. Furthermore, the code is well-positioned to play a significant role in the development of future modified gravity-specific galaxy formation models, as well as in the implementation of artificial neural networks in the context of the 2x2 covariance matrix analysis. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach can be used to estimate the degree of variation in gene expression associated with different traits and has provided novel insights into the biology of gene regulation across the genome. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the general theory of relativistic stars is the recurrence time of their companions, which could provide key insights. By analyzing a comprehensive sample of neutron star binaries that exhibit outburst patterns, our study seeks to establish whether the recurrence time of these systems is influenced by their spin or magnetic field. Alternatively, we investigate if it is governed by the binary's orbital period, as suggested by recent research on black hole binaries. Our study's findings indicate that the recurrence time of neutron star binaries is determined by their binary interaction rather than any inherent properties of the star, which has significant implications for the population of low-mass X-ray binaries and neutron star binaries within the Milky Way. In the case of the Galactic Center, these results imply that a substantial fraction of low-mass X-ray binaries and neutron star binaries identified in the region are actually inactive systems with outburst patterns that have not been detected yet. Consequently, there is a lower estimate of the total population of compact objects within the Galactic Center, which may have far-reaching consequences for the galaxy's history of star and black hole formation. Additionally, this study's findings are expected to impact our understanding of ultra-long period neutron star binaries on the outskirts of the galaxy. Furthermore, a distinction is made between two categories of neutron star binaries that exhibit outbursts: those with highly eccentric orbits and those with nearly circular orbits, as the latter are more likely to produce irregular outbursts with larger amplitude, as evidenced by the example of the GSJ171931-20364 system. Moreover, by analyzing the binary's orbital period and outburst patterns, it is possible to predict the recurrence time for those with highly eccentric orbits, as shown by the example of the ATOX J19145-6056 system, which is on the verge of entering an outburst. On the other hand, those with nearly circular orbits have such low probability of producing irregular outbursts with larger amplitude that their entire population is at risk of being misclassified as ultra-long period neutron star binaries. Those that exhibit outbursts with larger amplitude are expected to constitute about 30% of the total population of neutron star binaries that exhibit outbursts, as the entire population of these systems would otherwise be underestimating the total population of compact objects within the Milky Way by a factor of two. Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. Understanding these relationships is crucial for interpreting radio source data and predicting their polarization properties. The findings are relevant to radio interferometer observations and the search for radio sources in the Square Kilometre Array. The results provided are a useful resource for predicting radio source polarization in various environments. The research implies a link between the magnetic field strength of a radio source and its polarization properties. The study finds no correlation between the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra and source luminosity. geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity for multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This 
connection bridges Diamond--Sasaki's findings to earlier generalisations of 
Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects. 
Notationally, let $k$ be a positive integer representing the size of a 
Galois extension with an associated local ring $R$. Also, let $\overline{\rho}$ 
be a 2-dimensional Galois representation over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$, 
which is fully definable in terms of $R$ and has an Eisenstein family $\mathcal{E}$ 
with a specified weight $k$. Our study builds upon this setup to explore the 
relationships between geometric modularity of weights that are either algebraic or 
non-algebraic. 
Notably, in the case where the weight $k$ is non-algebraic, we establish that 
geometric modularity implies the geometric modularity of weights $k_i$, which 
happens to be lower algebraic conjugates of the non-algebraic weight $k$. 
On the other hand, if the weight $k$ is algebraic, we demonstrate that the 
geometric modularity of the non-algebraic weight $k$ results from the 
geometric modularity of its lower algebraic conjugates. 
This discovery holds significant importance because it bridges the generalised 
conjectures of Serre to algebraic geometry through the use of geometric 
modularity. 
Furthermore, our research widens the scope of Diamond--Sasaki's earlier 
generalisations to include weight $k$ that are not roots of an algebraic number 
and have a specific property.

geometric modularity of multiple lower algebraic conjugates, which provides a 
clear explanation for the relationships between the weights.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices. Specifically, a system based on an Intel Core i7-4790K CPU and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 GPU was used to conduct the analysis, with results showing that parallel processing can achieve close to linear performance gains, as evidenced by the formula P = (p-1)t_s + t_o, where P represents parallel processing time, t_s is sequential processing time, t_o is overhead, and p is the number of processing units. With this understanding, developing efficient matrix-based algorithms using parallel processing techniques becomes a valuable skill. To illustrate this point, an example algorithm for solving linear recurrence equations with variable coefficients was implemented using parallel processing, resulting in substantial time improvements over its sequential counterpart. Furthermore, this study provides a framework for introducing parallel processing concepts, such as the openMP system, to computer science students through the exploration of matrix multiplication. We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to build upon and improve previous work, particularly Huang et al's. GlossBERT model, which addresses WSD (Huang et al.,2019), we plan to enhance their results through modifications to their dataset, ensemble techniques, and replacing BERT with alternative transformer architectures like BART and ALBERT. A corresponding GitHub repository contains our code, which expands upon the original implementation provided by Huang et al. in order to yield enhanced WSD performance. Furthermore, our findings are presented in the form of an additional table integrated into their leaderboard. Our objectives are (a) to explore alternatives to the BERT-based GlossBERT model proposed by Huang et al., and (b) to showcase simple yet effective methods to improve WSD performance, which can be applied to any context where semantic variation exists. In the context of semantic word similarity, we employed the BERT-based baseline developed by Giancola et al. (2020) to compare the effectiveness of various neural network models. Our results indicate that both ensemble methods and alternative transformer architectures like BART and ALBERT outperform the initial BERT-based benchmark. Specifically, ALBERT achieved the highest score of 0.8996, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by 0.0496. Our research to enhance the GlossBERT model has the potential to benefit other structural semantic models relying on BERT, such as the Graph-Based BERT model described by Zhang et al. (2020). We are confident that our findings will motivate further research aimed at resolving the WSD issue. As a result, we are willing to collaborate with any researcher interested in exploring this topic by leveraging our results and extending upon our work. We have already established contact with one such researcher; from the University of Geneva, named Dr. Dina Springel, who expressed interest in co-authoring this paper with us at the EACL 2021 conference. However, due to scheduling conflicts, she regrettably could not attend the conference in person. Although we initially planned to present our findings orally, we were ultimately selected for presentation in the form of a poster instead. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual guides, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. When evaluated on a variety of logic-based reasoning tasks, models that excel at sequencing also demonstrate excellent skills in reasoning about temporal common sense and the ability to incorporate multiple forms of information. Our research offers valuable insights on the ability of machines to understand real-world procedures and provides a platform for developing cutting-edge machine learning models that can efficiently grasp the complex information presented in procedural instructions from multiple sources. In addition to the datasets and models mentioned above, our research is also accompanied by an accompanying website that showcases the sequential understanding abilities of machines and humans in relation to both written text and visual aids. The code for our models and the feedback gathered from humans are both available on GitHub under the term of CC-BY-4.0. Leveraging Guidance from High-Performance Models and Nearly 20K Human Feedback, We Successfully Trained a Machine Learning Model that Can Efficiently Sequence Real-World Procedures Defined by Combining Text and Images. The trained model's performance surpasses that of prior research and matches the sequencing abilities of humans. The model's performance was verified in a range of complex reasoning tasks. The study provides valuable insights on the ability of machines to understand real-world procedures and how machines can efficiently grasp the complex information presented in procedural instructions from multiple sources. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. The analysis reveals that the distribution follows a power-law with an exponential cutoff, similar to scale-free networks. However, the parameters of the distribution depend on the degree of the removed node. Notably, some node removals are equivalent to removing nodes with a degree of one, resulting in a cascade that conforms to a specific sequence. The association between these sequences and network structure may provide insights useful for immunization purposes. The theoretical model is verified through numerical simulations, and the results demonstrate the practical applicability of the model to real-world networks. The study concludes by highlighting potential research directions for further examining network dynamics using the micro-level approach. The previously unknown avalanche-size distribution of Cayley tree networks may have implications for understanding network behavior during attacks and other events. By analyzing the distribution of node removal sizes, researchers can gain a deeper insight into network dynamics. The study confirms that a power-law distribution with an exponential cutoff is a general property of networks that follow the configuration model. The model is applicable to networks with any degree distribution, and it provides a precise formula for the distribution of node removal sizes. The study concludes by highlighting the potential benefits of applying the micro-level approach to study network behavior during attacks. The model is a fundamental breakthrough in understanding network behavior during attacks, and it may be used to analyze the effects of any attack that removes nodes randomly. The study provides a clear definition of the terms used in the research, and it is a significant contribution to the field of network science. The model is a well-developed theoretical framework, and it is a key finding that the distribution of node removal sizes follows a power-law with an exponential cutoff. The study is a crucial step in understanding the effects of attacks on networks, and it may be used to analyze the effects of any attack that removes nodes randomly

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, this design may also provide insights for improving optical resonator systems in other precision interferometric measurements. The concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer can be implemented using existing technology in the next generation of global gravitational wave detectors, such as Einstein gravitational wave detector and space-based detectors like LISA+. The design is compatible with laser sources below 1 W power, making it suitable for a variety of detector configurations. Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity. Moreover, implementing this new protocol via a decentralized decision-making process across devices is also feasible and does not unduly strain the requirements for devices. Hence, this new protocol is suitable for large-scale MIMO systems in scenarios where many devices are present and space may be constrained. Analytical and simulated data are used to validate the new protocol's performance. Furthermore, the new protocol is compatible with devices that employ large MIMO arrays in random access procedures and can be employed in conjunction with a recently proposed scheduling algorithm. In addition to its applicability to MIMO applications such as TDOA, super-resolution, and channel estimation, the new protocol also delivers superior performance over traditional approaches in terms of algorithm efficiency. A key feature of this work is the derivation of closed-form expressions that characterize the new protocol's performance, obtain optimal parameter settings via a novel approach called the effective density, and demonstrate the new protocol's advantages over traditional approaches through a practical application called spatial frequency scheduling. A key aspect of this work is the development of an innovative decentralized approach called the density-evolved protocol, capable of efficiently managing a large number of devices. A significant contribution of this work is the creation of a new metric called the reception area density, a crucial property of devices that utilizes MIMO arrays. A further contribution of this work is the demonstration of the new protocol's superiority over traditional approaches through a practical use case called video transfer. A notable aspect of this work is the derivation of closed-form expressions that characterize the new protocol's connectivity, delay, and throughput performance. A significant contribution of this work is the investigation of different MIMO configurations as a way to demonstrate the new protocol's robustness. A key feature of this work is the development of an accurate yet simple method to calculate the reception area density.
