The issue of tailoring news to individuals' interests while respecting their data remains unresolved. Growing worries about over-collected data and its unintended use have motivated our research on balancing personalization and privacy. Our experience creating personalized content platforms that protect users' confidentiality has sparked an investigation into users' attitudes towards these topics. A conducted survey revealed the opinions of various age groups regarding personalization and privacy. In this research, we are sharing our key discoveries with publishers and the community to inform the design and development of next-generation news recommender systems, which should prioritize the human user and achieve a harmonious balance between personalization and privacy. Additionally, we aim to contribute to the advancement of technological solutions that support both personalization and privacy by publicly releasing our implemented code. This code is built on top of the widely adopted DuckTiled dataset and transforms it into a more versatile and user-friendly format suitable for both interventional and observational learning settings. This format, which we call RelationalDuckTiled, enables researchers to evaluate the effectiveness of news recommender systems through both quantitative and qualitative performance indicators. Furthermore, we have incorporated this new specification into an updated version of the renowned DuckTiled benchmark, which we have repurified as the RelationalDuckTiled benchmark. This new benchmark includes a cutting-edge implementation of our state-of-the-art dual-learning approach, which we used to develop the code that we are releasing with this study. This new approach uses both explicit and implicit feedback in a dual-learning setting to create a unified objective function that combines the results of two separate learning processes. This approach has yielded the best results in our experiments, which used real-world data to evaluate the performance of news recommender systems. These experiments demonstrated that both explicit and implicit feedback produced better results than traditional collaborative filtering techniques, while our dual-learning approach outperformed all other evaluation metrics. Moreover, we observed that the diversity of the recommended content had a more significant impact on users' engagement than their relevance. In light of these findings, we have redefined the evaluation metrics of news recommender systems to give priority to both diversity and confidentiality. This study provides a blueprint that other communities may adapt to develop their own next-generation recommender systems that balance personalization, privacy, and other critical considerations. This study is an invitation to both the technical and business leaders of the news publishing industry to join forces with us in creating a new generation of news recommender systems that protect users' data while delivering them the content they desire. This study is an open call to the broader research community

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented as a directed path with no crossings. The first method employs a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices. The second approach uses a 3-APSP-like framework in conjunction with SPQR tree-decompositions to provide a parameterized solution dependent on the graph's out-degree. The third approach, for graphs without bichromatic edges, uses a 2-APSP-like framework and Gaillard's single-source shortest paths algorithm based on treewidth to develop an FPT solution. We also demonstrate an NP-completeness proof for the bichromatic case and a general case when the graph contains only two edge colors. Additionally, we introduce a parameterized algorithm based on the number of edges requiring color changes to solve the Upward Planarity problem. Furthermore, this work is a part of the broader research on developing parameterized algorithms for planarity-related problems. We have previously explored such parameterized algorithms for several other problems, including Triangulation, Binary Tree-Decompositions, and Contraction Equivalence, and this work contributes new insights to the study of planarity-dependent parameters. We believe our research findings will be useful for further investigating the realm of planarity parameters and parameterized algorithms. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Consequently, our work also extends the reach of the universal operator growth hypothesis to volume-law entanglement and information capacity, confirming that these phenomena are inherent to any system where the Hamiltonian has Lie symmetry. Furthermore, our study introduces a novel method for optimizing the coherent state overlap technique, a widely adopted approach for studying operator growth and entanglement, by incorporating elements of matrix product operators and density matrix renormalization. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Furthermore, it provides the ability to identify and exclude dimentionally redundant dimensions. The LFDA R package is a comprehensive tool that encompasses LFDA strategies and provides a straightforward dimensionality reduction result visualization approach. The package is available on CRAN and can be installed through regular channel. The package source code is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengxuoye/lfda, inclusive of additional advanced features like Kernel Local Common Vector (LCV) and discussion on its properties. The package has been applied in the analysis of notifiable infectious disease data and in face verification experiments. The CRAN version of the package can be installed using the usual channel, while the GitHub version can be installed using the data("lfda") and then subsequent lfda::lfda() call. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The source code of our method has been made publicly available on https://github.com/bruno-oliveira-oliveira-Generalized-KMP. The paper has been accepted for presentation and publication at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2021, held in Canibal, Dalian, China, from October 17 to 23, 2021. Due to the pandemic, the conference was held remotely. Our work has also received the Best Conference Award at the IEEE/RSJ IROS 2021. EKMP has been featured in the cover page of its proceedings and in the official website of the conference. The paper has been selected for presentation at the Robot Learning Workshop & Competition associated with NIPS 2021, held in Vancouver, BC, Canada, from December 7 to 10, 2021. Due to the pandemic, the conference and the associated competition were held remotely. Our work has also received the Best Conference Award at the Robot Learning Competition & Workshop associated with NIPS 2021. The paper has been featured in the cover page of its proceedings and in the official website of the conference. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the pair-breaking effect caused by a strong Zeeman field by increasing the scattering amplitude of electrons, which may be controlled through chemical potential adjustment. Notably, the critical Zeeman field for spin-singlet topological superconductivity can be reduced to zero when Rashba coupling is optimal. Furthermore, we assess the impact of Rashba coupling on superconductivity using the mean-field theory, showing that it may also facilitate spin-singlet pair formation via Rashba-like processes. Our results provide a theoretical basis for realizing the spin-singlet topological superconducting state in the Rashba Hubbard model, which may be achieved with Rashba coupling strengths and doping levels that can be adjusted through chemical modification and interface manipulation. Additionally, we analyze the phase diagram of the Rashba Hubbard model with Rashba coupling, identifying potential risks of Rashba coupling-induced collapse into the Mott transition when attempting to create the spin-singlet topological superconducting state. Lastly, we propose that LaAlO$_3$-SrMi films, serving as Rashba coupling layers, may be used to create the requisite conditions for this particular phase. Nonetheless, further investigation is needed to fully understand the effects of Rashba coupling on the phase diagram of the Rashba Hubbard model. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors. Notably, this outcome agrees with the previously held understanding of the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in the cuprates. The study indicates that an earlier observed transition related to magnetism at high magnetic fields, specifically the magnetic field-induced transition in the underdoped La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_{4}$, is directly linked to this newly found vortex lattice structure transition. This knowledge can be utilized to look for this transition with the use of sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in the closely related material Y$_{0.4}$Ca$_{0.6}$Ba$_{2}$Cu$_3$O$_{10-x}$. This might offer a possibility to verify the 45-degree rotation of the square lattice structure by magnetic field, providing a means to explore the relationship between superconductivity and magnetism in the cuprates. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the concept of end exclusion zones has been implicitly incorporated into numerical simulations, a lack of systematic, analytical studies restricts our understanding of its implications. This study presents a detailed, analytical investigation to clarify how the size of the end exclusion zone influences brush regeneration and ultimately determines the pressure exerted on the adjacent surface. Our findings contribute to a more comprehensive knowledge of brush behavior and may also offer valuable insights for modeling biopolymers like actin or microtubules. Moreover, this research may facilitate the design of block copolymer brushes with desired properties, providing a precise regulatory mechanism to control brush regeneration and ultimate dimensions. A numerical assessment of our analytical predictions is conducted by comparing our results with the outcomes of extensive dynamical simulations, demonstrating excellent agreement and further validating our analysis. Our study may also be applied to interpret the results of force measurements conducted on strongly stretched brushes located between two plates, providing a possible explanation for the observed behavior in this scenario. This study may further be extended to consider the effects of surface tension, resulting from chain adsorption on the curved surface of a substrate, to control brush regeneration and ultimate dimensions. Additionally, this research may be used to evaluate the influence of a nearby wall on the behavior of an elongated brush located between two surfaces, representing a possible design for block copolymer nanoparticles with a high load-carrying capacity. This study may also be applied to understand the behavior of biopolymers like actin or microtubules, controllable in their structure due to their chemical composition, providing a possibility of controlling their properties. This research may be extended to consider brushes composed of objects with a high surface charge, subject to electrostatic interactions that may affect brush regeneration and ultimate dimensions. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We examine how this property changes as k increases from 1 to the greatest possible value for the graph. We also establish a method to calculate beta_k for any k up to a certain point, and identify specific graphs for particular values of k where this property jumps from being true to false. We confirm that the largest possible values of beta_k are reached at some point, and also prove that the order of the smallest sub-sets that achieve this property at different k can be reversed. We further explore how this property changes when we can measure the distance between points with more precise tools, and how it is connected to other similar properties. The definition of this property can also be applied to dynamic graphs and we discuss potential future research in this area. The name "beta_k" is suggested as the standard term for this property. The original name "truncated metric dimension" is also kept as it reflects the limitation on the distance between points. The term "truncated" is shown to be related to "skewed", "extended' and 'augmented" versions of this property. The name for the version of this property where the shortest distance between points is capped at some number k is put forward for the Graphs and Combinatorial Structures database with the prefix "TRIM". The database is searched for all types of sub-sets of vertices that are defined by a specific property, but only those related to the metric dimension are discussed here. The name for this property is also put forward for the conference IOWAGs in the listing of selected topics. The measure of this property can also be applied to the vertices of a graph rather than its sub-set, and this variant is defined as beta_k of the graph. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, it could complement targeted observations and missions dedicated to mapping the entire sky, such as CHAMELEON. Similarly, this method may be adapted for other telescopes, like the Fermi-LAT's successor, the Fermi-LAT2. To facilitate replication and improvement, they publicly release their modified dictionary learning code and pre-trained models on GitHub. These models perform impressively on the Fermi All-sky Survey, matching the actual data closely, and demonstrate robustness in the presence of transient sources; however, they require further optimization for handling variable sources. Moreover, this approach paves the way for combining Fermi data with that from other satellites, like the Gamma-ray Observatory, in the future. Additionally, they suggest employing a more realistic metric that reflects the actual performance of these models in detecting features compared to the standard root mean squared error. Furthermore, this study highlights potential collaborations and future paths for research, along with various applications for machine learning in astrophysics, such as analyzing broad-band spectra, detecting impulses, and identifying sources. As a result, they anticipate this approach to process Fermi data, along with any adaptations for other satellites, to be a valuable area for further exploration and development in the field of astrophysics. Therefore, they invite fellow researchers and any interested graduate students to contribute to this project, share their expertise, and participate in the development of this novel use for machine learning in astrophysics. In return, they are happy to offer guidance, provide access to Fermi data, and facilitate access to computational resources via the Fermi Partnerships and the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. Our initial analysis focuses on general combinatorial optimization problems; we then explore specific applications, including matching problems, facility location, and network flow, and develop efficient solution methods for these cases. We establish theoretical limits on the tractability of solving general combinatorial optimization problems using the serial dictatorship approach and examine the computational performance of this method on various benchmark instances from the combinatorial optimization library. Our results show promising improvements in solution times when using the approach on certain NP-complete problems. We also investigate potential connections between the serial dictatorship model and other well-known models of decision-making, specifically the marriage model and gas model, and discuss the implications of our findings for fair division in the presence of incentives. Our research provides a foundation for further exploration of the interplay between decision-making models and combinatorial optimization problems. We anticipate our results to be relevant to a broader range of optimization problems with multiple agents. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged objects, the most notable ones 
are binary asteroids PS1 Bin:2020-04-03$b$ and PS1 Bin:2020-04-03$d$, featuring 
an asteroid with a possible binary companion, where the primary component with 
an estimated diameter of 41 kilometers orbits the Sun every 715 days. This 
discovery is a significant advancement in detecting wide binary asteroids and 
enables future research on the binary asteroid population. It also enforces the
necessity to verify and refine the results provided herein, given the current 
limiting filter employed by Pan-STARRS, which might not adequately detect 
binary asteroids as effective as those involving larger secondary components. 
As such, analyzing future observations employing a system similar to that of 
the Pan-STARRS1, but with a different filter, is highly advised. It is also 
highly recommended to replicate the analytical approach presented herein on 
images collected by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. Doing so could
potentially increase the detection rate of binary asteroids by a factor of 
tenfold. Any newly identified binary asteroids discovered in this study have 
been submitted to the Minor Planet Centers' Binary Asteroids Project website. 
Furthermore, I would like to express my gratitude to having received financial
support from the National Science Foundation's Research Experience for Undergraduates program.

Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our model uncovers various folding pathways for proteins with complex knots and reveals the limitations of geometrical models in predicting the relationships between proteins with trefoil knots. Furthermore, our results suggest that proteins with twisted peptide chains may unfold through distinct pathways compared to those with random coil structures. Our research provides valuable insights into the folding processes of knotted proteins and sets the stage for a more comprehensive analysis of their behavior using advanced topological concepts. The accompanying trefoil knot database, constructed using our high-performance computational tool, is available for download and offers a wealth of data for further study. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. A link exists between the complex scalar field's effective potential, which gives rise to NG boson generation, and the distribution of zeros in the Zeta function, particularly in the case of the symmetric potential. Additionally, a comparison between the standard model (SM) of particle physics and its low-energy effective theory has been drawn from the perspective of NG theorem-driven symmetry breaking. A distinction has been found in their respective algebraic structures: the effective theory corresponds to a nilpotent algebra, in contrast to the non-nilpotent Heisenberg algebra observed in the SM. This difference provides a clear explanation for the phenomenon of massless modes lost upon going from the fundamental to the effective theory. Moreover, it has been shown that the symmetry breaking that gives rise to massless modes in the SM can result in massive modes within the NG sector, providing a mechanism for their mass generation. Nevertheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new contexts when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The DISCO framework may offer a viable path to creating resilient models that thrive in various high-stakes, real-world scenarios. When applied to topics like topics like hate speech and toxic content, our approach may provide a practical means to producing counterfactual data at a large scale, thereby enabling the development of more versatile and robust models that handle such issues with greater care. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the creation of highly lattice-mismatched materials and structures. Nevertheless, concrete evidence supporting remote epitaxy is scarce and is often supplanted by alternative explanations such as pinhole-mediated growth or van der Waals epitaxy. This study offers novel X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and scanning transmission electron microscopy evidence indicating that the Heusler compound GdPtSb grows through remote epitaxy on graphene, despite substantial lattice mismatches. Findings suggest that slight defects in the graphene substrate can lead to a switch from remote to pinhole-mediated epitaxy, and that this susceptibility to defects could be utilized to control film growth. The research contributes valuable insights to the understanding of epitaxial growth on low-dimensional substrates and may potential opportunities for the creation of novel materials and devices. Moreover, it highlights the potential of Heusler compounds, featuring unusual electronic properties, as bind layers in stack structures. Lastly, it presents an argument for the exploration of other materials that could exhibit a similar high degree of tolerance for substrate defects, thus enabling successful growth on various substrates including graphene. This knowledge may be utilized to control film growth to achieve a desired structure or to prevent growth altogether, giving consideration to potential future applications alongside the graphen or even within devices.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple GANs is a significant challenge, as it relies on the accurate assignment of images to pre-defined categories, which can be difficult when working with datasets that have a single positive label per image. To address this issue, a novel approach called Single Positive Multi-Label Sampling (SPMLS) is developed, allowing for the automatic generation of diverse multi-label samples from single positive labels.  By generating multiple potential labels for each image and selecting the most accurate one, a cycle-consistency constraint is introduced to ensure the diversity of assigned labels, which is achieved through a pairwise comparison of predicted labels.  To effectively utilize the automatically generated multi-label samples, a new loss function called SPMLS loss is presented, integrating the accurate assigned label, additional plausible labels, and a diversity indicator to refine the multi-label annotation.  Experimental results show that the proposed SPMLS method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating its capacity to accurately predict multi-label annotations from single positive labels, which can be applied to various applications such as image classification, segmentation, and retrieval.  The SPMLS method also exhibits potential in real-world applications like annotating medical images and has a user-friendly interface available at https://github.com/Alvin-EG/SPMLS.  By further integrating SPMLS with efficient optimization algorithms, the method can be applied to complex datasets with multiple positive labels per image.  The SPMLS framework has also been successfully applied to the annotation of face images, which can also be extended to the annotation of other objects like vehicles and body parts. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through GNS, by establishing an adjoint relationship. This relationship involves a higher-categorical extension that captures the relationship between GNS constructions for bialgebras and Hopf algebras, which finds a reflection in the Cho-Fung-Kennard result about the order of composition of functors in 2-Cat. This notion of adjointness provides a mathematical framework that underlies but is more abstract than the physical concept of an adjoint operation. We use this abstract framework to both prove the relevant mathematical theorems and illustrate the underlying mathematics using a simple example from physics. This work can serve as an advanced introduction to higher-category theory for physicists who work with algebraic QFT. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. Overall, our method offers a more effective and simpler alternative to the mean-variance model, reducing computations and eliminating issues with matrix inversion. We also explored how our score-based approach can be applied in practice, using real-world data and highlighting the benefits of its transparent and intuitive results. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our score-based approach can easily handle cases where some assets have negative returns and provide a clear framework for regulating short sales. We found that our method can significantly reduce the risk of losing money and produce portfolios with higher returns in real-world scenarios. Overall, our approach offers a more practical and reliable way to invest, outperforming the mean-variance model and reducing computations, complexity, and potential losses. In conclusion, our score-based approach is a more effective, simple, and real-world applicable method for modeling portfolio returns and designing performance metrics. It provides transparent and intuitive results, a clear framework for regulating short sales, and a more practical and reliable way to invest, producing portfolios with higher returns and lower risks. We believe that our method can benefit the financial industry, particularly asset managers, by creating a new score-based approach to evaluate and manage risk, design performance metrics, and make informed investment decisions. Furthermore, our approach can also be applied in other fields, such as biology, physics, engineering, and economics, by developing a geometric representation of the data, establishing a cumulative distribution function, and using score-based performance metrics. In addition, our method can be combined with machine learning techniques, allowing the discovery of hidden patterns in data and making predictions based on those patterns.

This study tackles a complex control issue where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs, building upon references [8, 12, 17, 18]. The current outcome is closely related to, yet independent of recent results established in [7]. The key technique employed involves a combination of probabilistic approaches, including the use of backward stochastic differential equations, as well as classical methods for deriving existence and uniqueness results for quadratic equations. The paper is an evolution of the authors' earlier results presented at the 2019 IMS-ABEICS conference in Tokyo. The updated proof provides a clearer path to proving the key result, by which the optimal payoff can be expressed as the supermersion of the minimum cost incurred when transitioning between states. This formulation facilitates existence and uniqueness of solutions to the underlying system of SDEs. The paper will be published in the 2022 volume of the Stochastic Processes and their Applications journal. The corresponding author of this paper can be reached at yann.ouali@univ-gueele.dz. To explore the significance of a new Leptoquark (LQ) particle, we investigated the production of an asymmetric LQ pair in hadron collisions using the Standard Model as a reference point. By analyzing the process $pp\to ULQ\bar{LQ}$, we determined the asymmetric cross-section's sensitivity to various LQ combinations and assigned it a symbol $\sigma_{\rm asy}$. The study demonstrated that certain LQ charges yield $\sigma_{\rm asy}\approx 0.1$ fb, whereas others yield $\sigma_{\rm asy}\approx 0.01$ fb. Here, we explore this problem's variants under its most basic form, where the goal is to find the sequence with the lowest Hamming distance to a set of observations, and we aim to identify all sequences that satisfy this condition. A key advancement made in this research allows us to establish a lower bound for the number of observations required, which depends on the number of sequences being considered and their level of similarity, as defined by the Hamming distance. A specific technique was developed to regenerate original sequences for two types of error sets: those with a single sequence as a nearest neighbor, and those with no nearest neighbor at all. Furthermore, certain patterns of error sequences were identified and a general method was devised to regenerate any sequence with a certain level of variation. All results obtained in this research have significant implications in various fields, such as evolutionary biology, phylogenetics, and computational biology. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval [0,1]. This conclusion results from analyzing the limiting dynamics of ASEP and obtaining an explicit, stochastic integral expression for the second-class particle's position. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which the second-class particle's velocity distribution takes specific forms, such as being uniform, bi-modal, or bounded. Additionally, we observe that in ASEP with "colored" particles, where particles are distinguished by their spacing from the second-class particle, the probability of the second-class particle moving at a given velocity is directly correlated with the density of particles at that velocity. This connection holds without the need for defining "microscopically relaxed" states. Our findings also demonstrate the existence of phase transitions in ASEP's system, where the second-class particle's velocity distribution undergoes an abrupt change in response to minor adjustments in the system's initial conditions. Lastly, we provide a probabilistic explanation for the uniform velocity distribution observed in ASEP, linking it to an exogenous "speed process" that the system's particles undergo. This connection holds analytical value and may be employed to explore other systems exhibiting similar behavior. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our approach's superiority is demonstrated through various image synthesis and reconstruction tasks, showcasing its potential to recover spatially varying surfaces, illumination, and geometric deformations on several datasets, including large-scale real-world images. The proposed shadow computation method also exhibits a significant speedup over previous approaches, achieving a substantial 5-10 times performance improvement. Our comprehensive evaluation includes both simple models and complex geometric deformations, and our code is readily available for public access. Through our results, we also explore the shadow computation method's robustness across various parameters and the effects of illumination visibility on image synthesis and reconstruction. The code is available at: https://github.com/stratican/spherical-renderer. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this challenge. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the model's ability to distinguish between patients with and without severe COVID-19 symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to various diseases, this approach is shown to accurately identify key components with clear paths from image data to desired outcomes. The proposed method validates the initial hypothesis by confirming that ICU admission in X-ray images of COVID-19 patients can be associated with specific lung characteristics. The models and techniques developed are also applied to two additional large COVID-19 datasets, with results indicating a strong link between certain lung features and a higher risk of ICU admission. Furthermore, certain respiratory system abnormalities identified in this study are found to persist even after correcting for lung injury severity, which could impact treatment strategies. The algorithms and techniques presented are made publicly available to facilitate further research in medical imaging, medical note analysis, and COVID-19 research. Due to their versatility, they can easily be adapted to other classification tasks. In the context of COVID-19, the results obtained highlight the importance of early detection through X-ray imaging, which could potentially inform and drive policy decisions affecting healthcare resource allocation. As a result, there is a clear need to consider incorporating AI-driven X-ray analysis as a standard component of pandemic management. The significance of early detection becomes particularly apparent in the face of rising concerns over COVID-19 variant waves caused by highly infectious mutations from patients who are severely ill and have not been diagnosed until their symptoms become apparent. In the future, researchers should consider collaborating with public figures and influential experts to disseminate the findings obtained from analyzing X-ray images, along with educational content on the importance of COVID-19 detection through imaging. During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA. With improved performance comes the potential for SABRA to be applied to additional VRD tasks that involve complicated object relationships. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. It consistently demonstrated superior or equivalent performance to all competitors, showcasing its effectiveness and scalability. One notable application of this approach is in monitoring continuous real-time traffic, which was also examined and showed promising results. The code for this project has been made openly available on GitHub. A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach that asks: may the government mandate the user reveal the passcode, specifically in scenarios where the user's knowledge of the passcode constitutes a crime or a violation of a court order? Our proposed framework, 'Don't Trust -- Verify,' aims to address this query by establishing a standard for the government's authority to compel a user to demonstrate that their device is capable of executing a particular function. This framework, in turn, paves the way for us to examine the viability of forcing users to demonstrate that their devices are encrypted or that specific information can be accessed. Through 'Don't Trust -- Verify,' we demonstrate that the government's authority to compel a user to decrypt their device is equivalent to its authority to physically inspect the device itself. Furthermore, we contend that this approach invalidates legislation such as the All Writs Act and the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), rendering them unconstitutional in regards to compelling users to decrypt their devices. Building upon 'Don't Trust -- Verify,' we introduce a second approach that enables us to differentiate between scenarios where the government can compel a user to demonstrate the capability to access certain information, from scenarios where the government can only achieve this by violating the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches. This second approach results in our conclusion that the government can compel users to demonstrate the capability to access certain information, such as executing a specific program or reading out information, provided that it does so through a legitimate means of issuance, such as a court order. Conversely, the government cannot compel users to demonstrate the capability to access other types of information, such as the content of encrypted files, without violating the Fourth Amendment. Ultimately, our approaches provide a framework for evaluating the constitutionality of legislation that compels users to demonstrate the capability to execute specific functions on their devices. Furthermore, we contend that any such legislation that forces users to reveal the capability to access certain information constitutes an unreasonable search, in clear contravention of the Fourth Amendment. Building upon our approaches, we introduce a third approach that enables us to explore the implications of compeling users to demonstrate the capability to execute a specific program. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Additionally, we included two appendices with supplementary analysis and calculations. Furthermore, this study provides a framework for validating and interpreting observations from the Kepler mission and the upcoming PLATO mission, and a method for identifying stars that exhibit complex internal rotation patterns. This complex internal rotation pattern could be an indicator of a star that has ingested a giant planet, and identifying such stars will provide a key to discovering exoplanets through asteroseismology. Additionally, this study highlights the possibility of detecting tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby nearby substellar companion, which could result from stars consuming their solid planetary cores. This study offers a series of future observational and theoretical studies to be carried out, including the collection of additional data with the PLATO mission, the development of advanced models that can predict tidal inertial waves, and the examination of potential links to field stars that exhibit similar internal rotation patterns. This study adds a new twist to our understanding of the evolution of lower and intermediate mass stars, specifically those that have undergone substantial internal mixing, and it provides a new target for the upcoming ESPADON mission. This study also provides a method for determining the angular velocity at the edge of the convective envelope, which could be used to identify stars that are in the process of converting their planetary systems, and it identifies a potential link between stars that exhibit complex internal rotation patterns and those that exhibit chemical anomalies. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Our work also highlights the importance of quantum regrouping, demonstrating that the shared classical correlations between two cavities must be transformed into quantum correlations in order to achieve multipartite entanglement. Knowledge distillation is a knowledge-transfer method where a proficient model (the teacher) trains a less capable model (the student) to achieve better performance. Traditionally, this approach requires access to the teacher's output on reference data; however, this study introduces a novel framework that enables a model to extract knowledge from a black-box model with whom it only interacts through classification tasks. The proposed framework based on meta-learning and reverse knowledge distillation successfully facilitates zero-shot knowledge distillation. We integrate this framework into a program that automates training for deep neural networks through zero-shot knowledge distillation. The proposed method is illustrated with experiments on natural language classification, where we substitute a part of the training dataset with data from a black-box teacher; the results demonstrate the advantages of this approach over conventional knowledge distillation methods. The code is also made available for public access. The proposed framework based on a model that takes input x and produces output f(x), when applied to input x and f(x), yields improved performance when f(x) is generated by a model of a different architecture or with random noise as the teacher. The framework is linked to observation bias, a well-known problem in cognitive science, and the code can be used for automatic knowledge distillation on large datasets. The paper further explores the potential of pre-trained models like BERT to act as black-box teachers, achieving high performance with just a small portion of the training data. The results on the GLUE benchmark validate the effectiveness of zero-shot knowledge distillation and the robustness of the model to different hyperparameters. The study also examines the role of classification bias in zero-shot knowledge distillation, showing that it is a crucial factor that affects the performance of the student model. The proposal of a new distortion method called reverse knowledge distillation, resulted in a significant boost in performance on datasets that are challenging to classify. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the knowledge transferred from a black-box teacher to a student model, and the results on the ReCoCo dataset showcase the advantages of zero-shot knowledge distillation over conventional knowledge distillation methods. The study also explores the potential of deep neural networks to act as black-box teachers for models that are difficult to train, achieving a high level of performance with just a small portion of the training data. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning using a new framework that learns a factored representation of actions, states, and rewards. Our algorithm, TRAIL, learns this representation by combining the expertise of 3 sources: a strong policy that makes the most informed decisions possible; a robust policy that can handle noisy data and prevent it from being misled by irrelevant or dangerous states; and a reward function that guides the learning process. Our method TRAIL achieves this by incorporating two auxiliary objectives that utilize both high and low-quality data. Our results show that our algorithm outperforms the current imitation learning benchmarks, specifically producing better max-accuracy performance, especially with smaller expert datasets. Our research also provides the first quantitative evidence to support the claim that suboptimal trajectories contain relevant information, which can be leveraged with our algorithm to produce strong results. On complex 3D tasks like playing air piano and driving, our TRAIL algorithm outperforms the existing imitation learning baselines, specifically exceling with smaller expert datasets. On the MNIST dataset, our TRAIL algorithm compares favorably to the current imitation learning benchmarks, especially with smaller expert datasets. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple domains in single-agent and multi-agent settings demonstrates CoIL's effectiveness, with significant improvements achieved through our approach over standard reinforcement learning and imitation learning methods. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. Our efficient data-driven method for determining action similarity boundaries also offers a cost-effective way to tackle large action spaces. Our ultimate model's application to parallel NMT yielded a notable 3.5 BLEU points gain, indicating that reducing the action space is a viable approach to enhancing RL translation quality. Our model's code has been made available on GitHub. Our model's name is Generalizable Action Selection (GAS) Policy, and we believe it has a positive social impact as energy costs associated with training massive NMT models can be reduced through our efficient approach, thereby supporting the sustainable use of computing resources. This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Furthermore, the relationship between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces is explored through the introduction of QFS-retracts and upper power spaces of QFS-spaces. Additionally, upper power spaces of discrete QFS-spaces are found to be equivalent to discrete FS-spaces. Moreover, the concept of quasicontinuous identities is explored, along with its connection to FS-spaces, revealing that the presence of quasicontinuous identities makes a QFS-space an FS-space. Lastly, the property of having quasicontinuous identities is investigated for upper power spaces, leading to the discovery that such spaces correspond to FS-spaces with the same density character. Finally, the definition of upper power QFS-spaces is introduced, along with its equivalence to discrete FS-spaces with the same density character. Therefore, the term upper power QFS-spaces is adopted to replace the earlier formulation. Additionally, upper power QFS-spaces that possess quasicontinuous identities are defined and their equivalence to FS-spaces with the same density character is established. Lastly, the concept of upper power QFS-spaces that derive from discrete QFS-spaces is explored, leading to the discovery that such spaces are isometric to subspaces of upper power spaces of discrete QFS-spaces. Finally, upper power QFS-spaces that derive from discrete QFS-spaces can be expressed as the closure of quasicontinuous identities in upper power spaces of discrete QFS-spaces. Therefore, the term upper power QFS-spaces that derive from discrete QFS-spaces is adopted to replace the earlier formulation. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. To address this issue, we experimented with a straightforward recommendation system that effectively reduced user exposure to biased news and resulted in a notable decrease in polarization across the group. Our research provides the groundwork for a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between user behavior, technology, and the rise of partisanship, along with concrete avenues for exploring additional aspects of this complex phenomenon. To facilitate further investigation, we're releasing an expanded version of our dataset that encompasses additional data and a more detailed analysis of online news consumption. By continuing to examine these issues, we aim to contribute to the development of more effective strategies for mitigating the adverse effects of increasing polarization and promoting a more harmonious online community. We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. It follows that the time complexity of solving V's word problem by a deterministic Turing machine is no more than $O(n^2)$, where $n$ denotes the number of generators in a given V word. This time complexity is currently the best known for V's word problem. We also explore the time complexity of solving V's word problem relative to multiple potential ordering invariants, and establish that this word problem can be solved in linear time when using a specific order, albeit this order is known to be uncomputable in general V contexts. We further prove that any of V's group generators share the same time complexity as solving a combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages. As a reference point, combined cyclic variants of two and three deterministic context-free languages respectively separate the space requirements of deterministic and nondeterministic Turing machines, with respect to V's word problem. This research provides the basis for a broader examination of the relationship between V's word problem and combined cyclic variants of context-free languages. It is our hope that this in turn will contribute usefully to the ongoing exploration of V's combinatorial properties. A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Our work also compares the recognisable sets in different base systems, including base p/q, binary with the 2-qth root function, and binary with the square root function. Our results demonstrate that all sets that are (p-1)q/2 recognisable in Bp/q can also be recognised in B2 with the square root function, while both can recognise all the finite, singleton sets, as well as the natural order relation, successor, and the qth root function. Although our analysis indicates that the reachability set of counter automata in Bp/q with q greater than two has a more comprehensive set of recognisable elements than base p/q with the same number of digits. Our analysis provides an automated method for converting base p/q systems into binary systems with the square root function, establishing both a theoretical and practical application of this concept. Our study offers a comprehensive framework for evaluating and comparing the recognisable sets in different base systems, providing a valuable tool for the field of counter automata and discrete arithmetic systems. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, prioritizing edge extraction while producing satisfactory texture representation. By prioritizing edge detection, EG-CNN module results in significant improvements in medical image semantic segmentation tasks. Specifically, our investigations demonstrate that an EG-CNN module outperforms a standard encoder-decoder network by a substantial margin when applied to the LIOSS dataset, yielding a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.879 versus 0.794. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that incorporating an auxiliary supervision block identified as the Edge-Gated Block (EGB) yields consistent improvements in medical image semantic segmentation performance, with a primary impact observed on organs with clear boundaries. As a consequence of our exploration, we conclude that a straightforward yet effective approach like the EG-CNN module can achieve superior results in medical image semantic segmentation tasks. The proposed EG-CNN module code has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. Moreover, we have introduced a new benchmark called the Liver Tumor Auto-Segmentation Challenge (LTAC) and made it part of the MICCAI 2021 conference, with encouraging outcomes obtained from participating researchers. Ultimately, our study paves the way for the further development of complex medical models featuring interchangeable CNN components, with our code and LTAC details openly shared on the Web. As a result, future researchers can benefit from the proposed EG-CNN module, as well as the newly created LTAC benchmark, to achieve outstanding results in medical image semantic segmentation tasks. Furthermore, the code and challenge information are readily available on GitHub and the MICCAI 2021 conference website, respectively, enabling other researchers to explore and build upon the proposed EG-CNN module and the LTAC challenge. Moreover, the comparison between our proposed EG-CNN module and other leading medical image semantic segmentation models has been made available on a separate paper, with the latter exhibiting state-of-the-art performance on the LIOSS, LiTS, TCIA, CVC-Clinic, and Liver116 datasets.

Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, eventually leading to the characterization of limit functionals and their associated energies. This characterization demonstrates how the original energy functionals decompose into two components: one representing the stored energy within the matrix, and the other capturing the energy accumulated within the fillings. Our analysis ensures that the limiting energy functionals satisfy the original differential constraints, thereby demonstrating the importance of constraints in the model. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our results to a specific scenario involving a particular differential constraint.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.005-0.047, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux compared to their total light. Observations indicated an average fraction of tidal light equal to 0.025 or 2.5 percent, with a standard deviation of 0.05. The distribution of tidal light was found to follow a Maxwell-Boltzmann form when considering the total light of the galaxies. No significant relationship between tidal light and the specific stellar mass of the galaxies was detected within the defined mass limits. Additionally, no correlation between tidal light and the degree of tidal interaction was found. Estimations based on the observed distribution of tidal light led to the calculation of a merger rate ranging from 0.01 to 0.03 mergers per billion years, with a 95 percent confidence interval. This research provides a statistical basis for studying tidal features in massive early-type galaxies and suggests that interactions with massive companions may result in a merger rate in the range of 0.01 to 0.03 per billion years, with a 95 percent confidence interval, which may be a key factor in governing galaxy evolution. Further investigation into a subset of galaxies with a high fraction of tidal light is recommended. Due to limitations inherent in the data used, especially when comparing their results to those from other studies, future research aiming to resolve small-scale tidal features will likely be facilitated by higher resolution imaging. A deeper understanding of tidal features in massive early-type galaxies may offer valuable insights, while identifying potential connections with galaxy scaling relationships that could provide a more comprehensive framework for studying galaxy evolution.
