The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of our approach in optimizing existing laser systems using genetic algorithms and the potential for inverse design of such systems in the future. We also release an open-source version of our software, named CPA-NLO-IDE, to facilitate collaboration and knowledge exchange among researchers and developers. With the increasing demand for high-power laser performance, our software model positions us to address the technical challenges facing researchers and developers working with CPA-NLO systems. Furthermore, it provides a solution for the reverse engineering of such systems, enabling the identification of optimal underlying parameters that yield desired performance metrics. With its modular architecture, our software model can efficiently handle the complex interrelation between CPA and NLO processes, and it paves the way for the development of advanced laser systems that incorporate exotic materials, such as graphene and semiconductor structures, as well as specialized thin film devices, such as waveguides and saturable absorbers. With its capabilities, we are confident that we can overcome the technical challenges associated with providing high-power laser support to scientific users and can PRedict, design, and optimize CPA-NLO systems with desired time-dependent electric field patterns, achieving the required energy levels necessary for successful user experiments. With our solution, we can tackle even the most daunting design, optimization, and reverse-engineering problems posed by the complexity of modern laser systems, and we can demonstrate the practical implementation of our software model in the development of a next-generation high-power laser system. With our approach, we can address any difficulty that may arise during the design, development, and implementation of CPA-NLO systems, and we can tackle even the most intricate time-dependent linear and nonlinear problems

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. These results demonstrate the potential of pre-trained language models like BART to achieve high-quality word ordering and suggest them as a viable method for other word manipulation tasks. Additionally, they highlight the importance of further examining the implications of relying on these models that are trained on vast amounts of text with a focus on linguistic aspects. The rapid dissemination of personalized videos on social media platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing marks in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network, comprising two parallel branches, collects domain-specific information and engages in a competitive minimization process to achieve optimal performance. Experiments conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate the efficacy of our method, with results indicating that our approach matches the benchmark's top-performing models. Furthermore, our method's capability to prevent the leakage of domain-specific information enhances its versatility, allowing for seamless adaptation to various input signal types (e.g., images, videos) with minimal modification.

As a result, the system's security is severely compromised, rendering it vulnerable to hack-ing. Consequently, this problem prevents the extension of existing proof-based security frameworks to cover cases such as PPRS. Our analysis reveals that an all-photon state attack, facilitated by PPRS or standard laser sources, can facilitate hacking into PPRS-based quantum key distribution systems, including those employing the quantum hacking proof-based framework known as "sifting angle attack." Furthermore, we provide an analytical approach to determining the minimum number of all-photon state attacks required to execute hacking into PPRS-based QKD systems. Our findings show that when the source is fully randomized, this number reaches a maximum of 0.5%, whereas it significantly surges to as high as 23% for the case where the source is subjected to minimal randomization. Additionally, we propose an novel approach to counteracting this type of attack, namely by incorporating an additional randomization step known as the "final randomization" technique, which is capable of reducing the number of all-photon state attacks to an acceptably low level of approximately 0.6%. Our analysis also indicates that when laser sources are employed, the system's security can be elevated to a secure level of approximately 10^7 with the current practical PPRS implementations, whereas superposed binary phase shifting sources can enhance this to a secure level of approximately 10^8. Nonetheless, it is essential to note that extensive experimental verification is required to validate these theoretical findings. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, it identifies further questions and potential approaches to the area of study. Moreover, the article introduces the concept of separating and equatorial angles in metric spaces with the property of betweenness, paving the way for its application to spaces with the property of fuzzy betweenness. Furthermore, the article raises the challenge of investigating category theory in the context of angle functions on metric spaces with the property of betweenness. Lastly, the article proposes the term "valley function space" to describe spaces with the property of fuzzy betweenness, which it deems a more appropriate term than the commonly used "fuzzy valley space". Additionally, the article defines the concept of valley isometry between valley function spaces and proposes the term "valley congruence" to describe the concept of equatorially preserving mapping between such spaces. The article expresses its hope that the introduction of these new terms, along with the previously defined terms, will facilitate the formation of a theorem within the category theory framework. We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for determining pressure. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment, it was then applied to the analysis of nitrous gas emitting from the exhaust system of a running engine, allowing it to accurately track pressure variations and composition changes. Notably, it was observed that increased backpressure resulted in reduced jet stability, reflected in pressure records, and notable pressure drops occurred at irregular intervals, correlated with engine cylinder firing events, accompanied by nitrous gas enrichment. Furthermore, it was discovered that enhancing oxygen intake by adjusting airflow could counteract the effects of increased backpressure on nitrous emission. This technique's effectiveness was also validated through the comparison of pressure measurements with those obtained using a highly sensitive pressure sensor. By incorporating time-domain measurement functionality, this approach overcomes previous limitations of rotational CARS, extending its applicability to a wider range of pressing scenarios. Additionally, this technique offers the advantage of pressure measurement during exposure to bright light, a limitation of other methods. Utilizing a high-power fs laser and an extremely sensitive detector enables the detection of extremely low levels of nitrous gas in air, a level that cannot be achieved with current methods. This technique's versatility allows it to be applied to the analysis of various gases, nitrous gas being used as a representative example. The unique combination of time- and frequency-domain measurement capabilities of this technique, coupled with its advanced detection system, makes it the most precise rotational CARS method to date, outperforming even the most precise fs/ps CARS systems in measuring pressure. Notably, this technique's time-domain measurement capability allows it to measure pressure in a single step, a significant improvement over previous methods that require multiple steps. Furthermore, this technique can measure pressure even when the measurement cell is exposed to bright light, a level that cannot be achieved with current methods. This technique's ability to accurately measure pressure in a time-domain CARS system, coupled with its ability to measure pressure in a frequency-domain CARS system, makes it the most versatile pressure measurement technique available. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by as much as $20$. The code for our research has been made publicly available on GitHub. By introducing a regularization term to capture inter-agent connections, we can adapt the framework to model relational data within each machine. This extension of DR-DSGD leads to a further acceleration in convergence, with a new bound of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K} + 1/T))$. However, this improved rate holds only if the regularization parameter is set to a relatively small amount, which may not be feasible due to potential computational issues. On the other hand, our preliminary experiments indicate that DR-DSGD can achieve a higher test accuracy than Decentralized SGD than without relational learning, although further exploration is needed to fully understand its benefits and limitations. As for future work, we plan to explore more robust variants of DR-DSGD and conduct thorough experiments across a broader range of datasets and networks. Moreover, we aim to integrate this framework into a larger framework for cross-domain learning called ATOM, and examine the performance of DR-DSGD on real-world applications with DR-DSGD. Additionally, we are going to explore more robust variants of DR-DSGD and conduct thorough experiments across a broader range of datasets and networks. In the near future, we anticipate publishing the augmented code of our research paper. Furthermore, we are considering submitting a conference paper that delves into the results and the underlying theory of our work. In the long-term, we are confident that this research will contribute to the development of decentralized learning frameworks capable of managing complex data sets. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Just like researchers before us, we employed a simulation cell that contains $N$ hard disks interacting in a random manner, where the pressure is calculated by measuring the force exerted by the disks on the walls of the cell. We discovered that even with a relatively small number of disks - for example, $10^5$ - and even with a simulation cell that is only moderately large in comparison to the disks themselves, there can be a rather significant discrepancy between our measured values of pressure and the theoretical value, especially when the space between the disks is measured in terms of the number of disks that would fit in that space. This phenomenon diminishes, however, as the number of disks in the simulation cell increases, and we were able to determine the precise rate at which the accuracy improves. We were also able to identify the underlying cause of this improvement - it is primarily due to the reduction in the magnitude of pressure fluctuations as the number of disks in the simulation cell grows. We investigated this by introducing an 'effective number of collisions', which represents the total number of disk-wall collisions that would be observed if the same number of disks were confined to a smaller simulation cell. As the actual number of disks in the simulation cell increases, the effective number of collisions rises in a stepwise manner, and we were able to pinpoint the specific values that yield the minimum pressure fluctuations. These results should be useful in designing computer simulations that accurately model the hard-disk model. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. The
code for our method has been made publicly available for review and use.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Specifically, it was found that one of these poles, originating from a collective motion, holds a relatively low width of approximately 2 MeV, whereas the others, resulting from fluctuations within core and quasicollective states, exhibit significantly greater widths. Furthermore, within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has shown that the width of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance cannot be solely attributed to the width of the residual interaction, as traditional theories suggest, but rather, it is influenced by the masses of intrinsic oscillations and collective motion within the nucleus. Additionally, research has demonstrated that the real part of a complex RPA eigenenergy, which represents the actual energy of the state, holds a disperse relationship with the RPA Hamiltonian's parameters, whereas the imaginary part, which denotes the width of the state, maintains a more straightforward relationship with the residual interaction strength and the density of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Therefore, studying the complex RPA eigenenergies within the RPA framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of excited states and their widths within nuclei. This knowledge can further be utilized to interpret macroscopic features observed in experimental data, particularly those resulting from elastic scattering, where the detection of a nucleus' excited states is performed on an event-by-event basis. Consequently, research on complex RPA eigenenergies can serve as a guiding principle for investigating other resonances within the complex energy plane. This involves searching for additional RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance, within the complex energy plane, as well as throughout the RPA spectrum, where landscapes of fluctuation components within nuclei await further exploration and discovery. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, this study showcases how this new approach can reveal underlying mechanisms and patterns that may not be apparent from data analysis alone. This new approach is also shown to compare favorably with existing state similarity measures, particularly in its ability to capture linear and nonlinear relationships. This study's findings and its proposed clustering algorithm are both of significant utility in their own right. As a result, the generator's improvement is hindered by its focus on distinguishing between the training data and non-training data. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. Consequently, it becomes feasible to detect the signatures of the highest energy physics within the context of the smallest-scale physics. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the induced spontaneous symmetry breaking can give rise to the required primordial abundances of light elements, as well as the observed density of dark matter, under specific conditions. Additionally, this model has the potential to incorporate gravitational interactions in a more integrated manner, comparing which to the conventional scenario, we find that the former has more stringent constraints, especially at higher mass thresholds. The model can also accommodate inflation, where it is necessary to select a particular mode to avoid the violation of the flatness requirement, leading to a specific prediction for the spectral index ('n=0.97') and signal ratios of different inflation fields, which can be verified or refuted by upcoming CMB experiments such as the 'PicoLSS'. The proposed model provides a potential explanation for the observed dark matter density, but it fails to adequately explain the COBE/DMR data, mainly due to an discrepancy between the predicted and actual amplitude of the anisotropy, which could be addressed by introducing a small logarithmic loop correction, thereby increasing the power at very small angles and thus matching the observed values at a much more precise level. The model also offers a possibility to identify the specific energy level responsible for the observed dark matter density, which could be probed by the LHC through the search for mono-photons, where it is necessary to select events with high missing energy and photon energy above 1 TeV, which could be achieved with an integrated luminosity of 100 fb^-1. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using resource selection functions (RSF).  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture (SCR) methods have enhanced capture-recapture analysis by incorporating space and capturing the complexity of animal movement patterns.  However, researchers are using traditional capture-recapture models more frequently than they are using SCR models to estimate density in conjunction with RSF.  This study investigates how to integrate capture data with resource selection functions by modeling the probability of animal presence in a given area, which is set as the starting point.  We examine two model-based approaches: firstly, we assessed if capture data can be used to refine initial population density estimates used in capture regression analysis; secondly, we explored whether capture data can be incorporated directly into capture regression analysis.  Our analysis suggests that capture data can indeed be used to refine initial population density estimates in capture regression analysis.  Regarding the second approach, we discovered that capture data can be incorporated directly into capture regression analysis, which provides the basis for incorporating spatial capture-recapture data into capture regression analysis.  This study provides the framework for exploring more intricate capture regression models that go beyond the case we analyzed.  We anticipate our research to be a starting point for investigating how to integrate capture data with other wildlife research methods that involve models of animal presence probability.  Finally, we discuss potential avenues for further research with which we hope to spur theoretical development.  This study is a collaborative effort between theoretical statisticians and wildlife researchers.  We are confident that our research will contribute to the advancement of the statistical capture-recapture field as well as to the effective management of animal populations.  In conclusion, we hope our study will inspire other researchers to explore alongside us the numerous avenues for further research we identified. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings. The novel approach employed involves an LP-relaxation and a sampling technique within the context of hypergraph cuts. This new algorithm can be modified to yield a simpler $O(\sqrt{k})$-approximation algorithm. Moreover, we determine whether an exact algorithm may be implied by this result, which would have far-reaching implications given the association with a long-standing conjecture regarding the tractability of certain graph classes. Notably, a $4\sqrt{2k)$-approximation algorithm would imply the tractability of searching for a smallest k-component in graph classes defined by non-trivial min-cut-classes. Conversely, proving the intractability of such problems would imply that no $O(\sqrt{k)$-approximation algorithm can exist. Notably, a k=4 instance previously established by Chlebik and Göös in their proof of P=NP for certain graph classes utilizes an exact algorithm implied by our results. Additionally, our new $4\sqrt{2k)$-approximation algorithm applies to Generalized Min-Power Connective Subgraph, a problem that encompasses various minimum power network problems, including those involving the formation of specific graph types, such as trees, sets of disjoint edges, and certain minors. The new $O(\sqrt{k)$-approximation algorithms we develop may also be applied to a number of specialized cases, including the formation of any k connective subgraphs with a minimum power criterion, the creation of a connected graph with a certain property using exactly k edges, and the development of a k-component with a minimum power criterion, subject to an additional connectivity constraint. Notably, an existing $4k$-approximation algorithm was previously available for some of these problems. The novel $O(\sqrt{k)$-approximation algorithms we present significantly improve the existing approximation ratios for such problems

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes that display non-extendible, persistent behavior as they propagate through complex networks. It is found that near the transition from localized to widespread activity, the system's properties are remarkably robust and are governed by a highly detailed balance principle. Additionally, it is demonstrated that a localized state of activity can emerge even in highly interconnected networks that are free from community structures. The models and methods developed in this research may be applied to investigate other dynamic processes that involve localization within network science. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. The revised approach may be employed with various methods for estimating the probability of game events, while the scaling of such probabilities enables meaningful comparison and differentiation of defensive strategies, encompassing factors such as team identity, gender, and national composition. The recently introduced SLIC clustering algorithm can handle complex data sets efficiently, but the time-consuming estimation of defensive valuations from broadcast videos containing unknown player identities, matches can result in clogged memory and high computation times. To rectify this, we introduced a pioneering method called K-Means with Encoded Bags, which facilitates the estimation of such valuations by clustering player subsets based on their encoded locations, resulting in significantly improved performance and efficiency. The innovative approach allows for the simultaneous consideration of instances of being attacked, scoring, and ball gain from large data sets, providing a groundbreaking solution to the complex problem of value-based location analysis in football matches. The novel algorithm may also be applied to location analysis in other sports and competition types, characterized by players with identical or varying identities, and broadcast videos containing unknown player identities, matches or types, which may lead to considerations of team, gender, national composition, player, match, type, and game event effects. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. Our findings indicate that HiP-RSSMs can accurately track changing trajectories and outperformed existing methods in multi-task learning settings. With its scalable Gaussian processes, HiP-RSSMs can handle a reasonable number of latent factors, typically five or fewer, making it an ideal solution for complex systems with numerous hidden variables. Our code is now available on GitHub, and the paper is currently under review for NIPS 2020. Due to space constraints, some additional details are included in the appendix. One significant improvement to HiP-RSSMs, the use of dynamic state occupation probabilities, was unfortunately omitted from the main text but has been successfully validated in the enclosed experiments. Although it may not offer a significant improvement over traditional state-space models in our present datasets, it has the potential to yield better results in data sets where state-space models would otherwise fail to converge. One such data set is the multi-task learning scenario presented in the eighth experiment, where the implementation of residence probabilities brings a welcome 15% reduction in the RMSE. The enhancement of HiP-RSSMs with residence probabilities may also provide a suitable basis for addressing one of deep learning's main drawbacks: its excessive memory requirement. As demonstrated in the enclosed visualization of the stochastic process, HiP-RSSMs can be likened to a sequence of nested containers, where each container represents a state's occupation probability distribution at a given time step. Although this structure, in itself, can result in a massive model, a significant compromise can be achieved by significantly scaling back the size of these containers. By doing so, HiP-RSSMs can be transformed into a highly efficient, lightweight model, capable of modeling even the most intricate time-series data, while also minimizing memory expenditure

While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and specifically, our proposed criteria classified 22 out of 24 previous results, alongside 8 out of 9 new methods, correctly into the desired categories. Furthermore, our model facilitated comparison across different measurement methods, captivating potential solutions to address the observed discrepancies, and notably, normalized space facilitated machine learning classification of in-depth polarized network characteristics. Additionally, our analysis provided insights on the fundamental elements that constitute polarized networks, underscoring the value of our approach for any scholar seeking to analyze the complex phenomenon of social polarization. Our analysis and our model are available online for further exploration. By standardizing the measurement of structural polarization, our results may pave the way for a more cohesive approach across different research methodologies. Furthermore, our study may offer insight to researchers working in related fields, such as community detection in networks, pseudo-absorbers in network dynamics, grapevines in information diffusion, and opinion dynamics in multi-layer networks, network resilience, and maligned influencer detection in social networks. Any scholar exploring these topics may benefit from our proposed criteria and our comprehensive evaluation of different measurement methods. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, this approach allows for the identification of active multilayer configurations that support solution existence. Our method is demonstrated through the analysis of a multilayer Kuramoto model, providing insights into how different layer connections impact solution dynamics. Additionally, our approach is shown to be a useful tool for multilayer network reduction techniques, such as the integration of inter-layer nodes that simplify multilayer networks into equivalent single-layer networks, by validating the resulting reduced models. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our new approach provides a more effective path to solving the initial data constraints and simplifies the process of constructing start points for numerical relativity simulations.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our data demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the conductivity and exhibits an unusual enhancement when subjected to a heavy metal layer interface. Furthermore, our research reveals that the anomalous Nernst coefficient can be decreased by means of electron scattering when an iron layer is introduced, presenting a promising pathway for optimizing this phenomenon. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN films, offering a basis for exploring other antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials. Additionally, our work highlights potential applications and potential uses of these materials in thermally activated magnetic switches and magnetic recording technologies. Our research was conducted with support from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the National Science Foundation, with additional support from the Army Research Office, the Department of Energy, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. The proposed test is an valuable linearity assessment tool for network autoregressive models.

A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This multi-faceted framework, which we will refer to as MFCModel, integrates elements from biology, thermodynamics, and mechanics to describe three key processes: sub-cellular reactions, cell-scale mechanical characteristics, and the cellular mass transport of proteins. This integrated model allows for the reassignment of common cell properties such as contractility, motility, and the relocation of proteins in terms of reaction forces, contractile forces, and the force of transport, making it a powerful tool for understanding how external stimuli affect the behavior of living cells. Additionally, this model enables the investigation of how the cell's internal components contribute to its overall locomotion and spreading by accurately capturing the intricate relationships between these processes. With its clear and consistent notation, the MFCModel framework can be applied to various cell types, providing a valuable tool for cell biomechanics research and showcasing the beneficial integration of biological knowledge and physical modeling. Furthermore, this model paves the way for further advancements in modeling the movement of proteins, contractility, and cell-scale reactions, which could be expanded to explore other multi-faceted processes in living systems. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models identifying parameters that influence the robot's ability to jump. Then, a feedback control system was developed to stabilize the robot's movement on the soft surface, leveraging its distinctive dynamics to optimize performance. When applying optimal control, the robot was able to jump higher than predicted models. This research demonstrated the potential of controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump on soft ground, a complex problem affecting robotics that could be addressed with modeling, simulation, and optimization techniques. This work may also provide a framework for solving problems related to robotic locomotion on soft ground. Additionally, it could aid the development of control systems using data from computational models and actual experiments on a hopping monopod, potentially extending to other robotic systems. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit numerical outcomes. These outcomes demonstrate how the nature of the meson interquark potential influences its form factor. It has been established that the impact of a vector meson's interquark potential on its charge radius is double that of a scalar meson. In the case of pseudoscalar mesons, the relationship is inversely proportional. These observations provide valuable insights into the interquark interactions that govern the form factors of hadrons. Additionally, the scope for the application of this approach is examined across the hadron mass spectrum. It is proposed that the contact interaction model can be applied to the study of baryon form factors, and a candidate for the $D_s^* (2510)$ meson has been identified. The results of this study are expected to facilitate a better comprehension of the internal structure of hadrons throughout the spectrum. Moreover, the derivation of meson form factors in this paper provides a framework for the investigation of hadron transition form factors and hadroproduction in high-energy processes. It is anticipated that the results of this study will contribute to a more intricate knowledge of hadron physics and will offer a perspective on the internal structure of hadrons, which can be scrutinized and validated with experimental data from various processes. Furthermore, the outcomes of this study can be employed to devise precise measurements in experiments such as the BESIII,CLEO-c, BaBar, Belle, LHCb, and ALICE. It is hoped that this study will facilitate the exploration of hadron physics from a different perspective, which is expected to yield new insights into the internal structure of hadrons. It is also anticipated that the results of this study will enable the comparison of experimental data from various processes, which in turn will contribute to a better comprehension of hadron physics. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. This study rectifies this by examining the droplet's interaction with aerosols. When the droplet is subjected to an oscillating electrical field, it initiates a flow of gas particles around it. The resulting gas flow patterns can be categorized into three modes: the droplet's surface becomes charged, creating an opposing charge in the surrounding gas that leads to repulsive forces; the droplet accumulates excess charge, resulting in a force directed towards the droplet's center; and the droplet loses charge, causing a cusp of repulsive force around its surface. The droplet's ability to manipulate its surroundings makes it a suitable model for various biological systems, such as plant stigmas and the surfaces surrounding certain fungal spores. The findings of this study could also contribute to the development of aerosol manipulation technologies, ultimately with potential applications in both biological systems and technological contexts. A video illustrating the droplet's interaction with aerosols is included with this study. By exploring this phenomenon, we aim to provide a theoretical framework that could facilitate the development of droplet-based aerosol manipulation methods, inspired by nature. A key aspect of this investigation is the use of a biologically relevant droplet size, specifically around 100 micrometers, which allows us to examine the complex interactions between this scale's hydrodynamic and electrical properties. To visualize the gas flow patterns, our setup incorporates a laser illumination technique combined with the analysis of aerosol suspension images. This study employs an electrical field with an alternating current component, which when varied, enables us to switch between different flow patterns by adjusting the droplet's charge state. A crucial factor in this research was maintaining a stable droplet charge over extended periods, which was achieved by controlling the electrical field, as well as minimizing the effects of external influences such as humidity and air flow. To further understand the droplet's behavior, our study incorporates charge measurement techniques, which provide valuable information on the droplet's charge state. By combining these measurements with the analysis of aerosol flow patterns, our setup enables us to fully interpret the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase. A key aspect of this investigation is the recognition that, in certain contexts, the droplet's influence on the surrounding gas phase is more significant than its response to the external electrical field. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our CONDAQA dataset is expected to drive the development of enhanced contextual reasoning capabilities within NLP systems, particularly when dealing with negation, a critical aspect of all human languages. To validate the generalizability of our findings, we conducted a series of cross-dataset evaluations, confirming that current models continue to underperform human evaluators on the implication inference task, even with the addition of additional training on more comprehensive datasets that cover a broader range of aspects of negation. Our CONDAQA dataset stands out due to its unique combination of attributes, namely the variety of negation cues, a focus on implication inference, diverse and challenging question types, highly accurate human performance, and the significant gap between human and model behavior. Ultimately, we believe that introducing this dataset along with our rigorous evaluation protocols will accelerate the creation of NLP systems capable of accurately processing complex texts featuring sophisticated negation in multiple languages. To support the exploration of numerous negation-related aspects, we also developed a comprehensive set of suites measuring the ability of NLP systems to comprehend complex texts featuring negation, encompassing not just implication inference but also other crucial aspects. These challenging datasets and our CONDAQA evaluation protocols are now publicly available for further investigation

In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Compared to flat-topic models, users prefer HDTM's hierarchical structure, with reduced mental processing effort and improved comprehension, according to our eye-tracking-based usability assessment. HDTM enables highly interactive visualizations, allowing users to explore and manipulate the underlying topic network, and our implementation of this is an interactive web application called TopicTree, which users find easy to use and efficient. With TopicTree, we identified salient document collections, encompassing influential papers on computer science and Wikipedia's most comprehensive articles, and their corresponding topic hierarchies, available at https://topictree.cs.washington.edu/. By developing a document-centric approach to topic modeling, we can create scalable models that capture the intricate connections in large networks, paving the way for a wider application of topic models in complex information networks. As our primary case study, we explore Wikipedia's topic network, leveraging Wikipedia's unique characteristics to define a suitable quality metric and assess the credibility of its content, and investigate Wikipedia's topical evolution, uncovering the enduring topics and new emerging ones, and analyzing the diffusion of knowledge through Wikipedia's pages. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system. This study investigates the relationship between the two methods, utilizing the example of the exact cover problem to illustrate their common underlying dynamics. Both parallel and serial quantum annealing techniques are utilized to measure the annealing gap, and this gap is found to correspond to the minimum of the Hamiltonian's spectral curvature in the system. Similarly, the quenching gap displays a similar temporal progression in its curvature, and both gaps are significantly influenced by the presence of non-interacting qubits. These findings suggest that the quenching gap can serve as a reliable indicator of a system's capacity for quantum annealing, offering a more convenient and universally accessible measure. Furthermore, this study reveals the pronounced impact of periodic driving on both the annealing and quenching gaps, leading to a fluctuation when compared to their stationary counterparts. This distinction highlights the distinct roles that stationary and dynamic systems play in the annealing process, and it is demonstrated that periodic driving not only reaches the ground state but also results in the system's membership in a mixed state. This study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between quantum annealing and quenching, and it showcases the utility of the exact cover problem as a model system for investigating this connection. Additionally, it highlights the need to address decoherence, which arises from the interplay between system dynamics and environment influence, and it presents a new perspective on the system's degree of entanglement and coherence as they evolve over time. Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. Specifically, it develops two new alignment measures for partial process runs, applies these methods to a case study involving software development processes, and compares the results with the process learning tool ProM-Align. The study shows that using partial process runs with alignments provides more accurate results and is more practical for use with real-world event data, which often contains incomplete process runs. The proposed techniques are available online for public use. Additionally, the paper addresses the issue of how to determine the most relevant partial process runs for analysis and presents a new alignment-based approach, along with the associated implementation. This new approach identifies the shortest paths in process models, which corresponds to the minimum required extensions for process runs, and is effective in identifying the most concise partial process runs for analysis. The associated code is openly available and easily adaptable for different process models. The study demonstrates the new method's effectiveness with a case study and showcases its capability to handle real-world event data. The study also explores new alignment measures for comparing process runs based on different process run lengths and provides the associated code, which enables the calculation of alignments for any process runs. The study further provides the code for a new visualization method for alignments, which enables the representation of partial process runs and can be applied to any process runs. The paper is related to recent studies on process variations, process-quality assessment, and data-driven process improvement. The study offers new techniques for measuring process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data, which is now available in the ProcessNet repository. The paper is well-structured and clear in its explanations, but can benefit from the inclusion of visual representations to illustrate the new alignment measures and the variable-length alignment algorithm. The study is comprehensive and covers essential aspects, but can be further enhanced by addressing potential limitations and constraints. The paper is suitable for submission to prominent process-mining conferences and journals due to its high-quality content, but requires the inclusion of additional sections on potential limitations, future research directions, and the study's contributions to pass the review process. The paper is 22 pages long, including the introduction, literature review, methodology, case study, results, discussion

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, this study shows that nickelate infinite layered materials are
amenable to a wide range of physics approximations, leading to diverse
phenomena arising from a single underlying model. 
Conversely, this implies that in order to fully capture the essence of these
materials, it is not sufficient to restrict oneself to a single physics
approximation, but rather all possible underlying models should be considered. 
As a result, we expect that any model that accurately describes nickelate
infinity layered materials will require a complex two-band or better yet,
multi-band representation. 
This work also holds a significant implication for the broader superconductivity
community, given that there are established grounds for criticizing the
conventional approach to superconductivity, namely that a given state is either
s-wave or p-wave, without any intermediate combinations.

correlation strength, whereas variations in the correlation strength rather
significantly alter the relative weights of the orbital's wave function.

This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections

different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. This approach, along
with the proposed algorithm, is presented and shown to be an effective solution,
as evidenced by our experimental results. Furthermore, our approach has the
advantage of being suitable for distributed memory systems, paving the way for its
further development and potential application in the field of software testing. We
also introduce the concept of temporal space models, providing a new framework
for understanding the temporal aspects of software systems, and four possible ways
of defining time-dependent software systems. Our approach, along with its proposed
algorithm, is compatible with both singular value decomposition and time-dependent
software systems, offering a more comprehensive solution for software system testing. This research is a step towards the integration of matrix factorization techniques and time-dependent software systems, presenting an innovative approach that, although initially developed for shared memory systems, is now adaptable to distributed memory systems. Our findings, obtained from both theoretical analysis and experimental results, validate the effectiveness of this approach, while also laying the groundwork for future research in the field of software testing. To facilitate further investigation, the proposed algorithm's code is available for reference. Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were employed to describe cuprate superconductors using their lateral connectivity. However, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths challenges this approach. Consequently, the inclusion of charge density waves is now considered, leading to an expanded class of tunneling models that can adapt to the unique characteristics of cuprates, specifically the relationship between interlayer transport and magnetic field-induced normal liquid. These models comprise two components: one describing transport within a single layer and another describing the tunneling connection between layers. The combined effect yields a non-linear relationship that varies with the strength of the tunneling and magnetic field. Notably, for strong tunneling or low magnetic field strengths, the models exhibit a linear response, aligning with the traditional tunneling model. The inclusion of charge density waves introduces a layer-width that affects transport, while the magnetic field effect is explained by the tilt of cupra layers due to strain from neighboring layers. The models provide a theoretical framework that can be tested through experimental measurement of interlayer transport and magnetic field-induced normal liquid. The proposed tunneling models are a significant advancement, offering a universal description of tunneling phenomena observed in cuprate superconductors, and the possibility of adjusting the models to fit the unique characteristics of different materials. The models also predict a strain-induced shift in transport layers, providing a new avenue for investigation. The description of transport phenomena provided by the models is highly comprehensive, addressing key aspects, including the relationship between transport and magnetic field-induced normal liquid, the impact of tunneling and magnetic field strength. The models can be applied to a broad class of tunneling systems, encompassing superconducting nanostructures and graphene, and the models can be further expanded to consider strain and temperature variables, enabling a complete theoretical description of the unique transport phenomena observed in cuprate superconductors. The models have significant implications for the design of superconducting devices, specifically the proposed tunneling model, which can be applied to any tunneling system, providing a new avenue for optimizing device performance by adjusting tunneling and magnetic field strengths. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a specific relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star that might be detectable through high-frequency pulsar bursts or soft gamma-ray repeaters.  Such stars would exhibit larger radii, smaller volumes, and lower magnetic fields compared to their neutron star counterparts, which could be verified through future observations of pulsars and black hole mergers.  Our research also indicates that sound velocity's expected behavior could lead to stars with masses in the range 1.8-2.6 solar masses, whereas the natural density relationships dictate a maximum mass of approximately 2.2 solar masses.  Any found star with this behavior should be reexamined, taking our findings into account.  Our work sets the stage for further investigation into the interface tension that governs quark star formation and could provide a new framework for identifying these stars.  Furthermore, it suggests that certain quark stars might already be accounted for in the current pulsar list, which could be confirmed through a more detailed analysis of their properties. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming. We provide an efficient polynomial-time algorithm to calculate a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a reduction similar to one used for Tai mapping, we can obtain a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between two trees in $O(|V_1|^{2.5}|V_2|)$ time. This anti Tai mapping framework contributes valuable insights to our study of Tai mapping and its association with other binary relationships between trees. We believe this new definition has the potential to enhance tree alignment methods and facilitate their extension to more complex domains. We further explore a connection between anti Tai mapping and tree stabilization, introducing the concept of an anti Tai path and providing an algorithm to calculate a maximum-weight anti Tai path on two trees. We anticipate that anti Tai mapping will become a useful tool in future research on tree alignment and related areas. With its potential applications in biology, legal document analysis, philosophy, and music, our new definition is likely to contribute significantly to the development of bioinformatics, legal informatics, philosophical informatics, and music informatics. Finally, we use anti Tai mapping to resolve a longstanding issue in philosophy, providing a clear answer to whether there can be multiple maximum-weight anti Tai mappings between two trees. We demonstrate this new concept of anti Tai mapping, along with its associated problems and applications, and show that it can be used to solve existing problems efficiently. We anticipate that future research on anti Tai mapping will lead to the development of new algorithms and methods, enabling maximum-weight anti Tai mapping to be calculated for more complex trees. We believe that anti Tai mapping will become a fundamental concept in computer science, facilitating breakthroughs in bioinformatics, legal informatics, philosophical informatics, music

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitudes are small may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters. Furthermore, both states exhibit parallel behavior as their properties evolve with anti-Casimir effect scaling in large systems. The identified combinations of squeezing and displacement could facilitate the creation of highly sensitive states using existing technology. The reference compass state, with specified parameters, can be created using a malidomide sequence of classical laser pulses on a driven system. The proposed class of states, with equivalent or near Heisenberg limited performance, may enable the development of large-scale highly sensitive state devices. Additionally, this class of states provides an opportunity to observe the anti-Casimir effect in large systems through shift measurements. The corresponding quantum circuit to produce these states is also provided. Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict one- and two-dimensional self-accelerating solitons. These models, based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, utilize a specific choice of magnetic and scalar potentials that form a dumbbell shape, providing a bridge between this specific scenario and general cases. The article also outlines a new method for potential applications, involving the use of potential landscapes to create "dark-solitons" in 1D and "ring-solitons" in 2D, achieved to some extent with Bose-Einstein condensates. The findings presented may contribute to a better comprehension of BEC dynamics, in addition to potentially guiding experiments to identify self-accelerating modes in BEC systems. The article also introduces a new term, "self-accelerating solitons," to describe this phenomenon, and investigators are encouraged to explore this concept with other BEC models. The article is also accompanied by a discussion on the distinction it draws between self-accelerating solitons and other moving solitons, as well as the relationship between this phenomenon and flat-banded models. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. To facilitate broader adoption, the SIMC 2.0 framework has been openly contributed to the ML library PyTorch. Experimental evaluations were conducted using ResNet-50, Inception-BN, and a custom Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). Moreover, the research investigates two common attacks, leading to the development of an enhanced protocol called SIMC 2.0-LP, and proves the security of this improved variant. Although SIMC 2.0 does not claim improved theoretical security, it has been shown that converting its protocol to a sequence of simple operations may provide improved security under specific conditions. Therefore, the research acknowledges this potential security benefit. Nonetheless, due to space constraints, the proof of this result has not been included in the paper, and instead is made available in the supplementary materials. Overall, the research focuses on enhancing the performance of private ML inference, with an open-source implementation available for exploration. To facilitate further advancement, the research also provides a theoretical analysis of existing solutions and proposes an appealing future direction called SIMC 2.0-Light, with an accompanying evaluation of existing solutions using the ResNet-50 benchmark. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. Additionally, this method allows us to establish that each element of a domain that can be represented as the sum of two squared components can also be represented as the sum of three squared components. This achievement is made possible by combining multiple techniques such as computing the class number, the ideal factorization of primes, and various applications of the non-hypothetical Weyl difference equation. As a result of this strategy, we are able to devise an algorithm for determining all possible non-trivial representations of an element as the sum of squared components. This algorithm, in turn, paves the way for developing a method for representing any element as the sum of two squared components - a technique that is already established for local domains and certain global domains. Furthermore, this method for two components has the added benefit of demonstrating that each element of these domains that can be represented as the sum of two squared components can also be represented as the sum of three squared components. This method is applicable not only to domains but also extends to certain global function domains. It is worth noting that this new method for two components relies on distinct principles that distinguish it from the previously established methods for computing the sum of two squared components. Additionally, this study explores the question of unique representations, establishing that unique representations exist for all elements of these domains (or function domains) except for specific prime indices. This achievement is made possible by our new method for two components, combined with the previously established methods. This study provides a comprehensive framework for solving the sum of squares problem in global domains and function domains.
