In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Furthermore, by comparing their results to those of Galtier, the researchers were able to validate his analytical predictions regarding the decay rates of certain statistical measures. In doing so, they provided a clear, quantitative proof of the existence of inertial wave turbulence and the associated Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum within a specific parameter range that characterizes turbulent flows. This breakthrough finding offers a powerful tool for testing any future theories or models of turbulent flows. Additionally, it provides a novel perspective on the long-standing issue of whether geostrophic vortices or turbulent flows better capture the essential properties of turbulent motion within rotating, stratified fluids. It is further shown that the latter holds true within the specific parameter range defined by the researchers. This outcome raises a question regarding what parameter value change could potentially switch the preference from turbulent flows to stable geostrophic vortices, with a corresponding impact on the underlying physics of the flow. Lastly, it is demonstrated that both artificial vortices and artificially created 'batches' of turbulent flows exhibit the same underlying physics, thereby further confirming the existence of inertial wave turbulence within a specific parameter range that characterizes turbulent flows. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the research also notes there are potential biases in the data without which the results could yield a 9 percentage point difference in recidivism rates.  To minimize potential biases, the analysis is repeated with a stricter data set that excludes offenders who were required to undergo mental health treatment but had it taken away by the court, as well as those who were not required to undergo mental health treatment but had it recommended.  Even with these restrictions, the data still indicates mental health treatment reduces recidivism, although the reduction is less pronounced at 3.4 percentage points.  The analysis also attempts to measure the impact of mental health treatment on future healthcare and criminal justice costs, assuming that providing mental health treatment to all eligible offenders would cost around $3,700 per person over three years.  Based on the observed reduction in future crimes, it estimates this could result in $11,000 in savings per person and three years or $3,667 in net savings per person.  The research concludes by noting that while it provides evidence supporting the effectiveness of mental health treatment for reducing future crime, it cannot address questions regarding the optimal length of treatment or the most suitable form of mental health intervention.  Furthermore, the study suggests that implementing Medicaid or other public healthcare programs for incarcerated individuals could provide a significant return on investment through reduced future crime.  However, the results indicate the data may not be sufficient to support a randomized controlled trial of mental health treatment due to the limited variation in court sentences, especially regarding treatment duration. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy, called the Interpolation Consistency Regularization (ICR) technique, uses interpolation to enforce consistency across unannotated pixels by comparing the predictions based on annotated and non-annotated data. This results in a regularization term that is computationally efficient and straightforward to implement. When integrated with convolutional neural networks, ICR offers a straightforward and effective way to utilize the implicit knowledge contained in unannotated regions. Our experiments demonstrate that ICR outperforms the current benchmark methods when the amount of annotated pixels is limited. Furthermore, ICR exhibits self-benefit when applied to cardiovascular segmentations, where it surpasses the state-of-the-art models in the DISEASE-Specific Partition (DSP) task. The code is openly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghliu95/ICR. The model has been thoroughly evaluated on the ACDC and MMWHS challenges, yielding top-ranked positions. The team of Dr. Liuiu, Dr. Zhong, Dr. Lai, Dr. Chen, and Dr. Liu participated in the 2020 ACDC challenge, ranking second in the publicly annotated subcategory and first in the privately annotated subcategory. On the MMWHS 2021 leaderboard, the team of Dr. Liuiu, Dr. Zhong, Dr. Lai, Dr. Chen, and Dr. Liu ranked first in both subcategories. The model has also been assessed on the NuScope dataset, achieving the best-in-class results. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This talk will detail the design of the full system, the development process of the board, as well as the results from the initial testing. This talk will be relevant to advanced digital design experts, particularly those with experience in the development of sophisticated digital systems for particle physics experiments. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform tailored for adapting deep learning-based knowledge tracing frameworks. By incorporating customizable data preprocesssing methods and unified evaluation metrics, PyKT enables transparent and reliable model assessments. This versatile framework facilitates a fair comparison across various implementations and allows for the exploration of key components affecting predictive performance. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and secure aggregation with robust protection against data breaches. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study introduces a new protocol that allows gradients with no bounds for convex and non-convex problems. By incorporating gradient clipping within the buffer aggregation process, FedBuffAsync provides a viable solution for optimizing models with large gradients, reducing the risk of explosion and improving convergence speed. Numerical experiments, conducted on random logistic regression and non-convex learning scenarios, demonstrate the efficacy of FedBuffAsync. Furthermore, a comparison with other asynchronous FedLearn protocols is included. Additionally, this study explores the effects of delayed updates and gradient explosion on the FedBuffAsync framework. A new clipping-based protocol, FedBuffGC, is also introduced as a baseline for unbounded gradient optimization. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found the minimum k necessary to create a sorting network with depth d by employing comparators of size k. Initially, we found that the smallest k adequate for any sorting network is k=3, as previously reported by several sources. However, we also discovered that there exist sorting networks with k as low as $\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil$ for certain values of n. Moreover, we established that any sorting network with this property must have a depth of at least $\lceil\sqrt{n}/2\rceil$ when n is an perfect square, or $\lfloor n/4\rfceil$ when n is not a perfect square. Our research also reveals the existence of sorting networks with k= $\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil$ and depth d= $\lceil n/4\rceil$. To achieve this, we employed a new combinatorial object, which we refer to as a k-element generalizer, as well as a novel application of the Chordless Cycles Conjecture. Our findings can be viewed as a part of a more general theory concerning the behavior of recursive networks. Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework using the REMI simulator, this study reveals that magnetic fields force gas to break apart earlier in mergers, causing non-interacting gas to collide and heat up, whereas stellar material continues in curved orbits. As the merger progresses, magnetic fields force gas to spread across curves, combining with stellar material to form extended bars and waves. This affects how material falls towards the center, reducing the likelihood of direct present-day observations of merging galaxies similar to those seen in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field. The findings of this study are comparable to those from similar simulations conducted by another group, providing insight into the magnetic field strength of present-day galaxy mergers. The results indicate that magnetic fields have a significant impact on the structure of gas and stellar curves during mergers, affecting how material falls towards the center and the visibility of these events from Earth. The study also reveals a correlation between magnetic field strength and the likelihood of observing mergers, with a probability of detection decreasing as magnetic field strength increases due to the absorption of electromagnetic waves, while the actual mergers with high magnetic field strength can be detected through radio waves. The outcome of this research will be used in a companion study on how magnetic fields are inherited by new stars formed during mergers. The legacy of this study includes providing parameters for setting magnetic field values in subsequent simulations, along with guidelines on how to differentiate between interacting and non-interacting gas in mergers, which can be applied to any similar simulations conducted using the same simulator. The study offers a perspective on how magnetic fields can shape galaxy mergers, while a companion paper explores the impact on the formation of stars and supermassive black holes, and another examines how magnetic fields are inherited by new stars formed during mergers. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that it yields pure Nash equilibria that are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to the specific values declared by the agents, while for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that it yields pure Nash equilibria that are fair allocations that are up to any good for any situation. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with declared values as input, pure Nash equilibria will always result in allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents. Finally, we investigated the challenge of achieving envy-free allocations in a setting with three agents and demonstrated that no mechanism will ever yield pure Nash equilibria that are fair allocations that are envy-free for this number of agents. All the results we obtained hold for valuation functions that are continuous and hold as well as discrete valuation functions. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic mappings to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This innovative approach enables us to achieve better results by generating more accurate and diverse samples during adaptation, ultimately leading to enhanced performance. By integrating our mapping method with adversarial training and a novel cross-domain mixture matching loss, we are able to demonstrate superior classification outcomes when compared to the state-of-the-art UDA methods. The code for our model is publicly accessible on GitHub: https://github.com/zwang84/Beyond-Mapping. The notation we employed for our results is based on the official evaluation metrics provided by the organizers of the domains adaptation competition, which included precision, recall, F1 score, mean intersection over union (mIoU), mean diameter (mD), and mean distance (mDis). The domain adaptation benchmark datasets used in our research are STL, Mini-ImageNet, and VGG-Segmenter, with the experiments being conducted on two different domains for each of the 12 unique domain pairs. The results we achieved outperformed the existing UDA leaders by a significant margin of 3.1% in terms of F1 score, 2.5% in mIoU, 0.015 in mD, and 0.25 in mDis. The notable improvement we observed suggests that the standard one-to-one mapping assumption used in previous UDA studies may not accurately reflect the complex relationships present in real-world domain transformations. The additional analysis we conducted based on the predictions made by our model, revealed that the classification of certain target domain classes could not be accurately achieved without the ability to undertake multiple mappings. Furthermore, the evaluation of our approach using the native target domain test set, yielded a notable increase in accuracy of 6.5% when compared to the existing UDA leaders. The impressive results we achieved provide a new benchmark for UDA models, with the approach we developed offering numerous potential applications, such as the enhancement of classification performance, solution to domain degenrate problems, and the identification of multiple mappings in UDA. Additionally, the innovative technique we developed could also be applied to other transfer learning settings, such as transfer learning with small data, transferring multiple sources to a single target, and semi-supervised segmentation. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. An attacker can observe an encrypted database before and after an update, allowing them to deduce sensitive information about individuals. We develop a new form of leakage to measure this risk. Building on the 'DP' framework from differential privacy, we show that it can effectively capture update pattern leakage. However, current research fails to consider update pattern leakage, which can lead to insecure update protocols and compromised user trust. To address this issue, we propose an update protocol that combines differential privacy with outsourced database updates, ensuring the confidentiality of update patterns, without relying on the integrity of the update patterns of users. This protocol first encrypts updates using a 'DP' framework, with an additional 'DP' application that protects update patterns from leakage. To improve efficiency, we integrate our protocol with an 'DP' framework that considers update patterns as auxiliary input, obtaining nearly the same efficiency as existing update protocols. Finally, we verify the security of our protocol using the 'FIPCoP' framework and demonstrate its effectiveness with real-world data. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation of our protocol. It can be adapted to address update pattern leakage in real-world databases, protecting the confidentiality of update patterns and upholding the trust of users. Furthermore, we identify scenarios that are susceptible to update pattern leakage and propose 'DP-Sync', an extension of our initial protocol. 'DP-Sync' ensures the confidentiality of update patterns in real-world databases through the incorporation of 'DP' framework, with an adaptation that considers the entropy of updates. This protocol, although more complex, can also be adapted to protect update patterns in batch updates and has been successfully tested with real-world data. Lastly, we outline directions for further research in the field of encrypted databases, with a focus on update pattern leakage and 'DP-Sync'. It is crucial to develop update protocols that protect update patterns from leakage, as it can compromise individual confidentiality and undermine user trust. Furthermore, it is essential to balance confidentiality with the efficiency of updates in outsourced databases. Therefore, it is vital to create practical and effective update protocols that safeguard update patterns, promoting the adoption of encrypted databases in real-world applications. The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios. These results were presented at the 42nd ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PDPL). In addition to feature importance, our work paves the way for a deeper understanding of prediction functions in Machine Learning models. To this end, we propose an intuitive language to express prediction functions and a corresponding type system that captures the core concepts of prediction functions, set to be further developed into a full-fledged static analyzer. This static analyzer will serve as a part of the larger framework we call Verdi, dedicated to building trust in the predictions made by Machine Learning models. This is especially crucial in secure and critical applications where the predictions of these models have profound consequences. By establishing a solid foundation of formal verification for prediction functions, we create an opportunity for a broader exploration of prediction functions that are provably reliable, with a view to integrating them into applications that require high security and stability. This is contingent upon the development of a suitable programming language that facilitates the definition of such prediction functions and an effective strategy for minimizing the computational expenses associated with the verification process. In the context of Verdi, this translates to the definition of safe and computationally efficient prediction functions that can be accurately validated, providing an opportunity for further investigation into this aspect. This work is a part of the Verdi project, aimed at building reliable Machine Learning models, especially in high-security settings where the predictions made by these models have far-reaching consequences. This is a topic of ongoing research, with numerous path forward, and the authors of this paper invite the broader research community to engage with this project. This project is a collaborative effort between the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the University of California, Berkeley. Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly accessible re-identification datasets, even if they claim to operate in an fully unsupervised setting, in order to leverage existing knowledge. This is not a viable solution since it restricts the scale to which representations can be learned in an unsupervised manner. Furthermore, it's not practical when applying the developed model to target domains where it has to compete with state-of-the-art models trained on labeled data. To address these challenges, we propose an entirely new, large-scale unsupervised person re-identification dataset with which to learn representations. Since the dataset lacks labels, we employ a self-supervised contrastive learning approach to train a person re-identification classifier. By doing so, we create a massive dataset ($1 billion$ pairs) of features that can be used for further self-supervised training or as a benchmark as is. When tested on a labeled dataset, a model trained on our dataset using only $10 million$ pairs achieved a $54.8\%$ improvement over baseline models, thereby demonstrating its potential as a source of high-quality features for person re-reidentification. When applied to target domains, our approach resulted in a $12.8\%$ average increase in accuracy and in some cases a $40\%$ reduction in the performance gap with models trained on the target domain on labeled data. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/eth3d/person-re-identification-billion-pairs. This work was done in collaboration with the Eth3d organization and involves a large group of participants who contributed to our dataset by annotating surveillance footage obtained from YouTube. In total, the dataset consists of $45$ hours worth of footage, containing $179$ different identities, and gathered over a period of $6$ years. When tested on the iJuke domain, which was collected after the annotations, our approach achieved a $49.0\%$ accuracy, and when applied to the Hero19 domain, which was collected $3$ years after the annotations, our approach achieved a $38.5\%$ accuracy. This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather opinions from a cross-section of the community through a survey that asks about optimal income inequality when chance factors are removed. The results show that, on average, a significant reduction in income inequality is preferred. However, this preference varies greatly among individuals, with some preferring a slight increase in inequality, but the main difference to note is how opportunities are linked to earnings. When the chance factor is high, most people want a greater decrease in inequality, but this desire decreases as the chance factor diminishes, leading to a U-shaped relationship between inequality and opportunity. The findings also vary based on how success is measured, with a surprisingly different outcome when the focus is on individual opinions rather than the community as a whole. Finally, our research reveals that income inequality can be understood through the lens of opportunity inequality, but this understanding may be limited to certain aspects, with implications for policymakers and social scientists. A notable aspect of our study is the way it measures the impact of chance factors on job success and earnings through a method called the Balogh-Kozma index. This approach was a key development in our research and enabled us to analyze the inequality-opportunity relationship effectively. Additionally, our study introduces a new way to examine how the opportunity inequality can affect income inequality, but this method is mainly useful when the underlying factors follow a specific statistical distribution known as a GARCH process. With these advancements, our study lays the groundwork for a more intricate investigation into the complex relationship between opportunity inequality and income inequality, including how other elements such as income volatility and social status might interplay. A new appendix in the revised version of our paper explores one aspect of this complex interrelation by examining how the relationship between opportunity inequality and income inequality might vary depending on the level of economic growth. This investigation is an important step towards a more comprehensive understanding of how different components of income inequality relate to each other and how they are perceived by different individuals. This revised version of our paper also addresses concerns raised by reviewers that the results based on the survey data might be influenced by the specific characteristics of the survey participants, by presenting a new analysis using a different methodology to gather opinions from a broader population. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. To facilitate widespread adoption of DataScope, its source code has been made freely available. The field of data debugging, specifically debuggers targeting training examples within comprehensive machine learning pipelines, is introduced and its current state characterized as the subject of the accompanying extended version of this paper. The term "Data Debugging" (DD) has been adopted to refer to this field, and its challenging problems, influential factors, and promising directions are outlined with attention to potential future research paths. The DD field is further explored through an interdisciplinary perspective, encompassing not just technological advancements but also practical applications and the societal implications of data-driven machine learning. The theoretical foundations of DataScope, the developed system for computing the Shapley value, are connected to the broader framework of computational model interpretation, a field in which the computation of the Shapley value plays a crucial role. The significant impact of DataScope on this field is reflected in the adoption of the DataScope Name and the inclusion of the system's description in an academic publication. Our research seeks to uncover the origin of radio sources within globular clusters through the use of kinematic information, instead of traditional color-mass criteria. We have analyzed 22 radio sources located within the core of the galaxy and within 10 kiloparsecs from the center, which are situated within 20 globular clusters. Among the 20 remaining radio sources, we were able to gather velocity measurements for 11 sources, while the others either had insufficient or unclear spectra. Our analysis indicates that a source's location, motion, and position within the cluster hold the key to understanding its origin. We have developed a multi-dimensional metric to evaluate these factors and predict the true nature of radio sources. Our results demonstrate that spherical expansions are a common occurrence within the galaxy and within globular clusters, while two-dimensional projections may initially suggest binary or impulse origins, which upon further analysis are found to be spherical expansions. Impulse origins are a less common scenario, especially outside of the galaxy's central region. Among the 11 sources with velocity measurements, we were able to identify nine that exhibited gravitational ties to the cluster, and among these, we discovered that five were subjected to tidal mass transfer, three were subjected to gravitational shaping, and one was a displaced source that was once a binary in the core. Our study provides a framework for identifying true binaries within globular clusters and paves the way for further investigation of radio sources that are truly binary in nature. This research is an expansion of prior studies and offers a different perspective on the issue, supported by data from radio archives, as well as observations conducted with radio telescopes, including VLA, VLBA, and ATCA. Our study sets the stage for a more in-depth analysis of the binary sources within these clusters, which will be the focus of upcoming research. Our primary tool for analyzing velocity measurements was the software package DOOP, while statistical analysis was performed using the scipy library. Our primary finding, that spherical expansions are a common occurrence within these clusters, challenges a widely held theory and sheds new light on the dynamic processes occurring within them. Our study also introduces a new way of evaluating the true nature of radio sources, which combines multiple factors. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel machine learning task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a 0/1 programming optimization method to reconstruct the hypergraph, while also introducing a flexible alternative approach that incorporates existing graph classification techniques. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our proposed methods and demonstrate their ability to successfully recover real-world hypergraphs from their graph projections, outperforming baseline models in multiple metrics. Our work's implications are illustrated through a case study on collaborative gift-giving activities, where our method identifies key groups of people more effectively than existing methods. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/linusrupp/SupervisedHypergraphReconstruction. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The code for our experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/learncodelearn/SIT. The SIT framework, in particular, demonstrates notable gains in multi-agent benchmark tasks, including achieving a 24.4% improvement in rating on the UMHLV Soccer dataset. The framework's effectiveness is further validated by a series of ablation studies, which reveal the significance of both attention and GAT components in obtaining optimal results. The analysis of our findings provides actionable insights for the selection of high-quality experiences in multi-agent offline learning settings. The scope of the SIT framework is extensively explored through a theoretical optimization perspective and a set of explicit policy updates, which can serve as a foundation for addressing more challenging self-play scenarios. We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results show this scheme outperforms standard approaches, especially in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of various factors including the duration of the yellow light, the driver's behavior, the automated vehicle's speed, and its following distance. These findings could facilitate the development of optimized connected vehicle control algorithms, critical for ensuring safety at urban intersections. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks. Key improvements made to the games themselves, in conjunction with various agent evaluation results, are also included. Furthermore, we've established a new benchmark for evaluating text-based game-related code and incorporated it into a fully open-source code repository called TextWorldExpress, available on GitHub. With the significant increase in simulation processing speed comes the ability to conduct a more diverse range of experiments, as shown by our investigation into multiple agent evaluation approaches. The findings indicate that certain methods can detect differences as small as a factor of two, which could stem from either the complexity of the games themselves or the limitations of the technology used. Overall, the development of text-based games as a means to assess virtual agents has a bright future ahead of it. The relatively simple text-based game interface also provides an ideal platform for testing natural language processing-related issues that arise when interacting with virtual agents through text, an issue often referred to as the "tyranny of the small step size" problem. To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Our results suggest that folding the spectrum or employing an imaginary time propagator shift can accelerate MSQITE, whereas unitary folding has a negative effect and decreases accuracy. Notably, we use MSQITE to correctly identify the lowest-energy state among multiple targets, which is not achievable with standard quantum computing applications. These findings demonstrate that model-space QITE is a versatile algorithm capable of handling a wide range of state-union problems. Finally, we apply MSQITE to the study of quantum magnets on frustrated honeycomb and triangular lattice structures, showcasing its potential as a reliable method for ground and excited state calculations in the study of quantum magnets. Due to its stability, model-space QITE is an ideal candidate to represent multi-electron ground and excited states in the study of molecular physics. In the case of nitrogen, we use MSQITE to accurately calculate the energy of the $\textrm{X}^2\textrm{B}$ ground state and the $\textrm{O}^2\textrm{D}$ excited state, which are critical for characterizing molecular spectra. Our results demonstrate that model-space QITE provides a trustworthy and consistent approach to modeling multi-state systems, which paves the way for its broad application in both condensed matter and chemical physics. As a result, this algorithm has the potential to become a leading solution for quantum computing applications involving the simulation of multiple states. Furthermore, due to its robust performance, model-space QITE is well-suited for integration with near-term quantum devices, such as superconducting quantum processors. In particular, we examine the potential for model-space QITE to be executed on the current generation of superconducting quantum processors, which offer a high level of control over the propagation of quantum states.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model provides adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, indicating potential benefits from implementing dynamic price discovery and fair competition in the redispatch market. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model is an adaptable tool that can be utilized to assess a wide range of design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex was also found to be associated with waves caused by the planet's rotation, which resisted the shift towards a more direct solar angle that occurs during Saturn's summer. These waves eventually broke through the vortex's surrounding area, creating the temperature contrasts necessary for its development. The vortex in the north is expected to continue forming every 15 to 17 years during the planet's summer. The Earth's atmospheric circulation, which is driven by the same type of waves that shape Saturn's upper atmosphere, may hold clues to explaining the planet's seasonal variations. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, states with low condensate fractions may be better represented by a superposition of quasi-condensation and fragmentation states. Finally, we propose that quantum double dark-soliton states could be created using laser techniques that induce notches in amplitude and phase. A specific protocol is provided for achieving a 1/3 filling quantum double dark-soliton state. Additionally, we examine the effects of a harmonic trap on these states. While a harmonic trap significantly alters the equilibrium behavior of these states, our study shows that it has a minimal impact on quasi-condensation, and that quasi-condensation and fragmentation will persist in these systems for some time. A numerical simulation is conducted to validate our finite-size scaling theory. This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3. This clarification involves Theorems A and B, which establish isomorphisms between geometric orbits, Kirillov measures, and Weyl groups' actions on these measures. These isomorphisms hold for orbits of nilpotent Lie algebra elements in sl2 and for orbits of certain elements in the Lie algebra so3. These results provide a non-trivial, algebraic basis for Altug's findings on orbital integrals from the geometric measure theory perspective. This involves an application of the above-mentioned Theorems A and B to a combination of measures, which yields a sub-group of the Weil-Deligne group as the group of characters whose compositions with the geometric measure of orbits lead to convergent integral estimates. This further enables the derivation of a specific formula for these integrals, which can be evaluated using a local function that is an extension of the gamma function, specifically the Langlands' absolute value function. This, in turn, allows for the computation of Tamagawa numbers as the product of local components. It is worth noting that this approach can be generalized to semi-simple groups and their orbits. Moreover, this research provides a geometric measure theory basis for Altug's findings on orbital integrals and measures, which forms the subject of her upcoming book. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout, producing phase diagrams that guide the minimum number of errors that can be tolerated in a repeatable process. Furthermore, we investigate and model the effects of malfunctioning parity check circuits, demonstrating a fundamental threshold below which quantum error correcting codes can successfully protect quantum data, even with the most sophisticated and optimized variants of the topological Shor code. This breakthrough was achieved by addressing two specific types of errors - a single systematic error and a specific type of statistical error, separating the classical parity check error correction process from the quantum code itself. This understanding may facilitate the development of futuristic quantum computing architectures that can execute a vast number of parity check circuits, crucial for topological quantum computing, with significantly improved performance. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. Furthermore, our method allows for significant reductions in spatial degrees of freedom, achieving this by utilizing the dimension-reduced approach for the blocking fractures. This resulting scheme can be solved using anililating Krylov methods, such as GMRES. Our method's primary disadvantage is the dimensional switching technique's limitations, where the Raviart-Thomas mixed finite element method's robustness is compromised when modeling conductive fractures. This is an area where further research is required, to fully explore our method's potential. Our approach has also been implemented using the FEniCS Project, an open-source computational platform. This implementation is set to be made freely available to the scientific community. Ultimately, our study's findings are intended to contribute meaningfully to the development of efficient, accurate numerical methods for modeling single-phase Darcy flow within fractured porous media. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist. The utility of our generalized version is illustrated through its application to the Heisenberg algebra. Specifically, we have obtained a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists for the Heisenberg algebra, confirming that all such twists can be obtained from a 1-cochain. The resulting one-parameter family of Jordanian twists includes both the standard Jordanian twist and the Q-deformed twist. The former arises when the parameter $q$ equals $e^{\theta}$. In contrast, the latter occurs when the parameter $q$ is set to $e^{i\theta}$. The utility of our approach is further demonstrated by its ability to yield local twist maps for the one-parameter family of Jordanian twists. The formulation of our derived one-parameter family of Jordanian twists in terms of $r$-matrices is also presented. The connection between our approach and the Bi-bracket structure arising from the one-parameter family of Jordanian twists has been explored. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual word embedding models. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our model and data are available at https://github.com/ghrua/cluster-consistent-embeddings. Our code is based on the PyTorch framework and the open-source 1000 Languages WordSpace, encompassing 14 languages used in our experiments. The initial production measurement of various particles like pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Moreover, a notable rise in proton-to-pion
ratio is observed as centrality decreases, with the $\phi$-to-pion ratio showing a 
centrality dependence expected for a hadronic decay product like $\phi$. Systematic
analysis of particle ratios in relation to charged-particle count is novel and 
enables the interpretation of particle production as essential, regardless of 
whether primary or decay products are considered. Therefore, our research permits
the use of charged-particle count as a crucial factor to understand particle 
production in heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the adoption of a non-strangeness
selective fragmentation function can be validated with experimental data, 
providing a theoretical perspective on particle production that needs further 
clarification. Moreover, our study paves the way for investigation of the 
centrality dependence in a same-multiplicity context in large systems like p-Pb 
collisions, with a key consideration being the choice of reference system. Our 
results encourage a comparison of particle production in the same-multiplicity Xe-Xe
and Pb-Pb collisions to further uncover the nature of particle production in heavy-
ion collisions. Additionally, our research justifies the use of Pb-Pb collisions 
as a reference system to study production processes in small systems like p-Pb and 
pp collisions, with a focus on same-multiplicity comparisons. Our study also 
opens up a discussion for investigation of the centrality dependence in a same-multiplicity
context in large systems like p-Pb

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The models trained with ASSIST achieve top ranks on all metrics in the DialogStateTracker Challenge of DialogSummit 2021. The source code of ASSIST is publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-CLGShop/tree/main/assistant/assistant_dialog_state_tracking.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this, the model was expanded to incorporate individuals' willingness to travel in search of looting opportunities, incorporating this feature may provide a more precise depiction of rioting in Santiago. However, further validation and refinement of this extended model are necessary. A key modification made to the model, representing population movement, raises ethical considerations, thereby it is not being made publicly available and details of the modified model are being shared with individual researchers. It is essential to note that this project's primary objective is to contribute to the development of a mathematical model that could potentially predict and manage the spread of riots, a critical issue with the potential to cause widespread damage and disrupt social order. Furthermore, this study may provide valuable insights for authorities tasked with containing and mitigating the impact of riots. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an innovative, training-friendly and efficient VIO model, based on the external memory attention mechanism, able to process cross-domain information and learn movement patterns, resulting in robust and efficient estimation of agent pose. Experimental results show its superiority to existing VIO learning-based methods, particularly in challenging scenarios and without the use of outdoor training data. The source code of the proposed method is made available online. Further, to facilitate the evaluation of VIO learning-based methods, a comprehensive dataset including difficult real-world sequences, is also made publicly available. The results obtained with the proposed method and nine other state-of-the-art learning-based VIO methods, using the newly created dataset, are also shown. The recently created dataset, in addition to adding diversity to the currently available VIO datasets, includes not only challenging man-made sequences but also natural scenes, such as forests, where the agent may move back and forth, as well as beaches, where the rotation of the agent can exceed 360 degrees, and different types of stairs, including those with non-flat surfaces, where the agent can move forward and backward. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Furthermore, FedSA demonstrates a favorable performance compared to other decentralized models, showcasing the advantages of its controlled aggregation method. As a community, we hope that by exchanging models via FedSA, we can accelerate progress in computer vision, while mitigating the risks associated with interconnected, globally connected network architectures. To facilitate further research, we have made the FedSA dataset and customized PyTorch code publicly available. Through FedSA, we aim to establish a secure framework for the collaborative development of neural network models, enabling researchers and organizations to contribute to the community's knowledge and expertise. This initiative has the potential to revolutionize the way we collaborate, allowing for the creative amalgamation of diverse knowledge and skills. This opportunity is particularly valuable in the context of artificial intelligence, where collaboration can give rise to novel, combined capabilities that might not have been possible through individual efforts. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Our ultimate aim is to discuss the implications this research holds for future theories seeking to explain grid cells' functioning. Through in-depth analysis of past studies, we hope to provide a comprehensive perspective on the current state of grid cell research and the expertise that has been gained over the past decade. This knowledge of grid cells can be further utilized to better understand these cells' significance within the brain's neural network. This survey is an adaptation of a previously presented conference paper and is now being made available as a full-length published study. This decision was driven by the realization that recent advancements in grid cell research contain breakthroughs that were not reflected in our initial presentation. This revised version of our paper includes a more comprehensive exploration of key aspects related to grid cells. This extended examination of our findings has provided us with a clearer understanding of these cells' underlying mechanisms. This newfound insight into grid cells has sparked a new question in our minds. We believe that our research, coupled with the expertise gained from studying grid cells, might be employed to guide the development of future neural network models. This guidance could be instrumental in helping these models navigate the process of being trained on real-world data, thereby enabling them to better grasp the underlying concepts and principles. Firstly, we determine the minimum rank of a matrix $A$ that allows all rank-$r$ matrices with positive or negative entries to be transformed into a symmetric form with at most $t$ rank-$r$ errors. This condition holds if and only if the rank of $A$ meets the criteria $r \leq (t-1)/2$. Secondly, we develop an efficient decoding algorithm for correct errors in cases where the error matrix $A$ has a rank no greater than $(k-1)$, where $k$ represents the code's rank. Additionally, we establish connections between rank metric decoding and other well-known decoding problems, including the resolution of a long-standing open question related to Gabow's 1980 publication. Our research's main innovations are described in an accompanying survey focusing on recent advancements in rank metric decoding. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can accurately pinpoint the source direction of an X-ray transient in just 2 exposures, which is a significant improvement over the 7 exposures required for a single LE unit using a single image sensor. The MuLE concept can significantly reduce the total count of image sensors required in a wide-field X-ray monitor employing LE optics, which in turn can reduce the system's total mass, volume, and power consumption. As a result of this reduction, there is more onboard storage and communication bandwidth available for the detection and monitoring of X-ray transients, which is the system's primary purpose. The proposed MuLE design can also serve as a tracking camera for X-ray sources monitored by an X-ray telescope using a large detector on board the same satellite. The MuLE design using a single shared image sensor can, however, introduce a potential dead time when switching between different LE sections. This dead time, which is currently set at 10 milliseconds, might need to be optimized based on the specifications of the actual image sensor used in the design. Furthermore, our analysis facilitates the development of a practical implementation for real-time signal classification, which is crucial for multi-messenger astronomy. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Furthermore, we make the annotated EMO20Q data set with revised labels, along with guidance on the proposed evaluation framework readily available for public access. In addition to enhancing the quality of the EMO20Q data, our method's potential to guide annotation processes guided by neural models is a key area for further exploration. In the context of the BERT-Assisted Annotation Framework, which we introduce, we discuss incorporating additional neural models with distinct characteristics, such as diverse BERT variants, which could aid in the annotation of specific data sets, thus expanding the scope of the method to other types of annotation tasks. By applying the BERT-Assisted Annotation Framework to EMO20Q, we aim to pave the way for the co-evolution of high-quality annotated data sets and sophisticated neural models. Experimental studies are conducted with multiple BERT-based models, covering both the annotation evaluation and revision processes, and the results obtained are presented and analyzed. Finally, considerations for future research and potential lines of inquiry are presented. We anticipate the proposed approach to contribute positively to the advancement of both emotional intelligence and question answering technologies. In the process, we raise the question of whether evaluation and refinement procedures similar to the one detailed could be incorporated into the training process of modern neural models, thus giving rise to a new direction for exploration. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. Further analysis of the entire asynchronous polar sample, however, revealed that the majority of hard spectrum detections belong to a small sub-group featuring short spin periods, which could indicate a relationship between spin period and X-ray spectrum. Notably, the smallest of the short spin periods (P_orb/2) are more commonly found in the harder spectrum detected asynchronous polars, suggesting a possible link between very short possible accretion periods and more intense X-ray emission. The possible implications of these findings on our understanding of asynchronous polars, specifically the idea that they might exhibit more persistent and larger amplitude X-ray outbursts, are discussed. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This could also extend to detecting minute changes in a superconductor's critical temperature or its transition width, potentially facilitating the assessment of high-temperature superconductors. Furthermore, this method may provide a means to enhance magnetic resonance imaging of superconductors by utilizing atomic sensitivity to measure these fragile states of matter. The system's functionality can be validated with a demonstration of $1.6 \times 10^{-3}$ radian accuracy in atomic phase measurement, a component crucial to overall performance. The described setup can be adapted to detect the residual local magnetic field in atomic systems by incorporating additional shielding. Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a specific subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  Additionally, DynaSOAr's memory management efficiency is compared to the memory allocator of Microsoft Visual C++ 2015, showing that its memory usage is sometimes 5 times less than the baseline.  The framework's simplicity and flexibility have also enabled us to explore new memory allocation strategies, such as allocating memory in blocks, and we have successfully integrated it with the CUDA OpenMP (COO) hybrid programming model.  With DynaSOAr, we have successfully parallelized a range of challenging real-world programs, including a leading video game, and have made its source code available for public use. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects.
