As a result, we were able to successfully reconstruct clouds using just one of the nine MISR cameras, which could potentially be achieved from board a low-Earth orbit. The improved approach, using an efficient forward solver developed in collaboration with the Los Alamos National Laboratory, took around 30 minutes of computational time. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target first, whereas the lower frequency component interacts with it last. Consequently, a more complex and persistent SIPT is established, leading to increased and persistent energy gains in ions. Notably, at specific phase matching conditions, a significant amount of energy can be transferred from the laser to the ions in just one plasma layer. The model we presented can be utilized in designing optimal laser pulses for efficiently accelerating ions through SIPT. Our research provides a theoretical framework for further study on the dynamics of interacting laser pulses with varying frequencies with targets at the relativistic SIPT threshold. We propose utilizing more intricate laser pulses with designed frequency variations to achieve greater energy transfer efficiency from the laser to the ions. Our analysis indicates that such optimized laser pulses can successfully bypass the limitations imposed by linear variation assumptions, enabling a deeper exploration of relativistic SIPT dynamics. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Finally, calculations using the B3PW721 hybrid functional yield results aligned with our primary findings, providing a means to potentially reproduce such outcomes via smaller supercells.  Nonetheless, errors associated with Ti 2p core-level photoemission following TiO2 doping, specifically discrepancies in experimental measurements utilizing this method, remain an area of ongoing research.  We contend that TiO2 should be re-examined as a reference point prior to studying the effects of doping, as both its band gap and magnetic properties may be affected by core-level photoemission.  Furthermore, variations in Ti-O bond lengths following doping may also be a contributing factor to such discrepancies, as they directly impact the positioning of Ti 2p core-level levels.  We propose utilizing both experimental and theoretical methods to fully understand the causes of such errors, with a view to regaining accurate results in studies utilizing this method. I demonstrate that using a combination of theoretical predictions and experimental data, we can accurately identify this process by examining the momentum distribution of protons in the forward direction. Furthermore, I illustrate the feasibility of this method with the current LHC energy levels and proposed future upgrades. Additionally, I outline the advantages of this method over conventional detection methods and highlight potential opportunities for breakthroughs in top-quark pair production and light jet polarization studies. Furthermore, I illustrate the scalability of this method for use in proposed future colliders such as the Future Circular Collider.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. The advantages of using qudits are attributed to the increased precision offered by multi-level systems in measuring the distance between states. To illustrate this benefit, we provide homogeneous networks as a scenario in which qutrits offer little improvement over qubits in this aspect, whereas the advantage of using qudits is evident in the case of heterogeneous networks. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a massive 1024-bit static ISO, and a 16kHz sampling rate. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter is varied, often in a way that simplifies the problem. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and super-renormalizable theories in future work. This study is a part of a broader project that aims to explore the relationship between fluid dynamics and the renormalization group, an area that has been examined at a theoretical level. However, this work represents a major advancement in the field, especially given the non-trivial numerical evidence it provides in favor of the idea that flow equations embody a concept akin to the advection-diffusion of physical observables. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. Despite the significance of this task, it remains a persistent challenge due to issues like noise reduction, cloud thickness, and the varied characteristics of LiDAR data, which can differ significantly from other sensing technologies. Advanced classification methods such as feature selection, forest-based models, and neural networks have been explored in recent years; however, a comprehensive review of these developments and a clear distinction between relevant and irrelevant methods is lacking. This study examines the fundamental techniques of feature selection, assesses the performance of various forest-based models, and evaluates the benefits of using neural networks on LiDAR data. Our research indicates that even basic composite feature selection methods surpass baseline performance, while also demonstrating the superiority of multi-layer perceptron over other classifiers. Furthermore, our analysis provides insights into the effectiveness of LiDAR data when compared to the classification of multi-sensor point clouds. Our experiments also raise important questions regarding the optimal middle elevation angle for LiDAR sensors and potential links between cloud thickness and classification accuracy. Our work paves the way for the advancement of LiDAR point cloud classification through the exploration of new techniques and the public availability of our comprehensive classification benchmark. Our benchmark includes an evaluation of modern LiDAR sensors, a detailed description of cloud characteristics, and a rigorous examination of classification performance across various forest types. This significant step forward has the potential to drive breakthroughs in the classification of LiDAR point clouds, addressing key challenges and outperforming existing methods will require further examination of feature extraction methods, the reevaluation of common assumptions, and a deeper understanding of the underlying physics and cloud characteristics. Our research positions the classification of LiDAR point clouds as a leading problem in machine learning, with a potential real-world application showcased in our collaborative work with environmental stakeholders. Our study highlights the benefit of incorporating raw LiDAR data into classification systems, achieving this is crucial for the continued development of accurate and robust classification methods, as well as meeting the evolving requirements of applications that rely on LiDAR data, such as forest assessment, where the classification of thin trees has become a key challenge. Our analysis also emphasizes the need for the open exchange of cloud data characteristics, which is essential for the advancement of classification

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. As a result, one-step recurrences can be established for the expanded coefficients of zonal functions, making it possible to utilize established libraries of positive definite functions for new applications requiring a specific space dimension. The developed framework is then applied to several contexts, including the construction of new kernel functions and the determination of operator weights for variational principles. The developed framework is particularly useful in the field of potential theory and harmonic analysis on the sphere. The invented method allows obtaining new kernel functions and determining operator weights for variational principles, thereby enriching the repository of positive definite functions up to dimension five. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are utilizing extensive air shower arrays and neutrino telescopes to join forces and jointly analyze their data. By doing so, they can identify neutrino sources and locate the origins of UHECRs at the same time. The IceCube Neutrino Telescope has observed several UHECR-neutrino correlations, though the statistics are currently limited due to the rare nature of these events. Presently, the largest dataset available is being analyzed by a collaboration of researchers, who have discovered a significant UHECR-neutrino excess in data collected between 2000 and 2017. Specifically, they observed UHECR sources of neutrinos originating from large-scale structures, specifically from the positions of nearby galaxies, whereas pre-existing analyses had found no significant deviations. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The implications of our findings are relevant to multiple fields, including food industry processing, pharmaceutical production, and the management of natural disasters caused by landslides and earthquakes. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Our method achieves comparable performance to gamma attention while using a standard attention architecture, and notably outperforms gamma attention itself when data augmentation is applied, resulting in substantial gains of 1.03-1.05 in NIST BLEU scores and 0.16-0.20 in WMT BLEU scores. Our model also exhibits smooth and interpretable attention distributions, particularly with data augmentation, where a notable example reveals a clear target word 'influence' on the choice between two words. We believe our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism to be a significant advancement over conventional attention models, and our results encourage the exploration of targeted generation models in neural machine translation. As a result, there is a pressing need to mitigate artificial biases that emerge from the application of attention models, by designing new attention mechanisms that can effectively handle such challenges. A Unified Dark Fluid Model was previously developed to combine the effects of dark energy and dark matter. This new model varies in density based on the gravitational field it's within, reflecting the dissimilar behaviors of dark energy and dark matter under rapid expansion and local gravitational fields, respectively. The model's cosmological implications were initially assessed using a perturbation approach, but recent studies suggest that these variations could be caused by a dissimilar cosmic fluid response to gravitational and scalar vibrations. Therefore, this paper proposes a new framework for the Unified Dark Fluid Model, based on a fluid description that accounts for both gravitational and scalar vibrations, leading to a density that responds differently to these vibrations. This new framework successfully explains the Universe's present-day large-scale observations, and it predicts specific scalar vibrations that the Universe should exhibit on medium to large scales, making it a testable prediction of the model. This new approach to the Unified Dark Fluid Model involves modifying the four-speed hypothesis, introducing different speeds for gravitational and scalar vibrations, with potentially far-reaching effects on our understanding of the Universe. This new model also offers potential to be applied to other contexts, such as the Large Number Problem, and it poses a more complex problem for modeling the Universe than a constant four-speed, but it has the advantage of describing the Universe's dynamics through an ordinary differential equation, in contrast to the fractional derivative equation of the original Unified Dark Fluid Model. However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as it is a prerequisite for deep and long-term learning.  Although technology can enhance curiosity, a lack of standardized methods to measure this trait through learning technologies hinders the development of effective tools.  Our research addresses this challenge by presenting a multifaceted approach to measuring curiosity in university students working in pairs, as well as assessing the validity of their measurements. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience. Further information on the package can be found at the package website. 

### Strong Consistency of MFSSA Estimator

The strong consistency of the MFSSA estimator is established under the assumption that the multivariate functional data are independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and the eigenvalues of the kernel matrix vary at a rate defined by the spectral distribution theorem. Conditions for the spectral distribution theorem are relaxed in the context of MFSSA, addressing a notable challenge in the field. The theoretical framework also provides insights into the factors that influence the asymptotic consistency of the MFSSA estimator, including the choice of the kernel matrix, the dimension of the domain, and the number of data points. 

### Numerical Studies and Real-World Applications

Extensive numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of MFSSA, comparing it to other dimension-reduction techniques such as multivariate functional principal component analysis (MFPCA). The advantages of MFSSA are illustrated through multiple scenarios, including the analysis of multivariate functional autoregressive (MFAR) processes, Gaussian processes, and residual-based dimension reduction. Furthermore, MFSSA is applied to real-world datasets, including intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. The implementation of MFSSA enables the identification of functional loadings and the dimension-reduced subspace, providing a clear and intuitive visualization of the results. 

### Implementation and Availability

The MFSSA algorithm is implemented as an R function, accompanied by a detailed user guide and a comprehensive documentation. The implementation of MFSSA is designed for flexibility and ease of use, allowing users to specify various parameter settings, including the dimension of the domain, the number of singular values, and the type of kernel matrix. The Rfssa package, hosting the MFSSA function, is made available for public use, along with a dedicated website providing package documentation and usage examples.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attribution patterns or characteristics of manipulable data, thus enabling the identification of suspicious scores with higher effectiveness. Furthermore, we explored the benefits of incorporating a de-biasing module within the scoring model to reduce the development of biased models caused by imbalanced data sets. The proposed solutions can be applied across a wide range of automated scoring applications requiring the evaluation of written work. The code for our methodology can be found at https://github.com/andersonbatista/AES-Probing. The autoscoring models used in this study are available upon request. The findings of this research provide crucial insights into the complex behavior of deep learning-based automated scoring models, uncovering the underlying causes of their sensitivity and instability. By successfully addressing these challenges, we can ensure the reliable use of these models in critical decision-making processes. The expertise gained through this research can be transferred to other domains where similar issues may arise, such as the detection of credit card fraud or medical diagnosis.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As an innovative approach, our project combines refinement types with the unique properties of blockchains, incorporating a custom type of termination proof obtained from refining types to verify that a Michelson program is useful. Additionally, HELMHOLTZ includes a novel form of counter-model construction, derived from a combination of monotonicity and termination, that identifies incorrect programs. For instance, this feature on Teranish-Ishihama's Faintest Core, an extension of Core Type, yields a counter-model demonstrating how to make the core type assignable. With a focus on user experience, our verification tool includes an interactive user interface enabled through Tezos' Ligo development environment, making it easier for users to incorporate HELMHOLTZ verification into their program development process. Furthermore, Michelson's expressive power, enabled by its reflexive types and operations with effects, also enable HELMHOLTZ to verify a program with a specified property, even if the program is more complex than what is originally expected. As a result, this project opens up new possibilities for the development of blockchain smart contracts with refinement types. For instance, this possibility of verification allows for the creation of programs that, while not terminating, still produce interesting outputs, such as programs for solving NP-hard problems approximately. With its successful integration with Ligo, this project also makes it possible to combine Michelson with other development tools, such as the Coq proof assistant and the Catz tool, enabling the verification of a Michelson program through Coq and subsequent compilation to Ligo with Fst2, and finally executing the program on the Tezos blockchain with Catz. This project is now an official part of the Tezos repository, available for use and further development. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. We also demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by applying it to a real-world parking lot scenario. As part of our method, we develop a general framework for defining outcome-based value functions, which can be utilized in multiple state representations. This new framework allows us to incorporate various state space descriptions, such as spatial coordinates, edge connections, and learning-based representations,, making our hierarchical method broadly applicable. We anticipate our hierarchical framework to contribute positively to future research aimed at efficiently managing large-scale discrete stochastic game theory-based simulations. We publicly release our implemented code for reference. Thanks to our hierarchical approach, complex grid world stochastic games can now be solved as multiple smaller-scale games, which we anticipate will facilitate collaboration with experts in computer vision and robotics who use learning-based state representations. Furthermore, our code can serve as a reference point for the development of future search-based deep reinforcement learning methods. We are also exploring potential extensions of our hierarchical framework to handle multiple evaders and pursuers in the future. We could utilize spatial autonomy to collect more precise outcome values for each state, which could enhance the performance of our hierarchical model. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ must be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. 

We demonstrate that the likelihood of a 'cyclic' triple being 'nontransitive' is at least 25% more likely than the likelihood of the triple being 'cyclic', with this difference reaching 50% for'strictly 'cyclic' and'strictly nontransitive' triples. 

Our study of a broad class of models, which we refer to as our main model but can also apply to models based on the less commonly used Copula approach, provides the basis for our results.

A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the generator is able to efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image. The results of our experiments clearly show that the new model matches or surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art cycleGAN-based methods, while also achieving a major reduction in memory usage (by approximately 6 times) and a significant decrease in computational time (by approximately 6 times) without the need for any optimization techniques. As a result, the new model is highly suitable for a wide range of memory-constrained CT datasets. To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei. Furthermore, we observe under conditions typical of halo nuclei, the elastic properties of rotational states generally follow the deformed rotor model's predictions. However, in the case of $^{44}$Mg, significant inelastic components within the halo structure lead to distinct elastic properties, underscoring the importance of considering the continuum for an exhaustive comprehension of distorted halo nuclei. Our findings also suggest that configuration cross sections can serve as a crucial indicator for identifying shape decoupling effects, providing a research direction for the experimental detection of such phenomena. By examining rotational characteristics in continuum systems, our study paves the way for a further exploration of superfluidity phenomena in distorted halo nuclei. Finally, we propose that $^{44}$Mg serves as a valuable test case for studying the relationship between an object's intrinsic structure and its elastic properties when rotating rapidly. Nonetheless, due to spin alignment effects, it is likely that coupled collective and single particle motion will continue to be pronounced even at high angular momenta, an aspect that merits further investigation. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and straightforward applicability to both single-frame and multi-frame super-resolution, making it a versatile solution. Our project has been made publicly available on GitHub, showcasing impressive before-and-after visuals of video super-resolution results. With our improvements, BasicVSR++ has emerged as a leading state-of-the-art model in the field. In comparison to leading competitors at the ECCV 2020 Video Matting Challenge Leaderboard and the Common Video Super-Resolution Benchmark, our model has consistently demonstrated superior performance, with results available on the project GitHub repository. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The research also yields an estimate for the screen thickness, suggesting it is significantly smaller than the Earth's distance to it. The findings provide valuable insights into the interstellar medium near the Sun and offer a new perspective on the morphology of the Local Bubble. The prescribed strategy for detecting such screens can be applied to further pulsar scintillation studies. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency information via pitch-dependent dilated convolution layers. Secondly, a pitch-dependent stochastic layer is integrated into the QPNet architecture to generate spectral contents based on the given frequency magnitude. Experimental evaluations show that pitch-dependent dilated convolution layers significantly improve modeling performance for unseen frequencies and the combination of this network with a stochastic generator matches the audio quality of the full QPNet model. As a result, a compact, efficient, and high-performance generative model is derived, referred to as Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet). The extended version of this model, incorporating multiple pitch-dependent layers and a global generator, is referred to as QPNetwork (QPNet-UC). This QPNET-UC model is selected for a public evaluation trial and proves compatible with popular music information retrieval frameworks. The source code of the proposed QPNet models has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository specified in the author list. The proposed QPNet-UC model exhibits superior performance to WN, Multi-Scale WaveNet (MSWN), and Transformer-based generative models (TFGN) in objective quality assessment tests. The results indicate QPNET-UC outperforms the competitors across all frequency bins and demonstrates a notable advantage in high-frequency components. Notably, QPNET-UC achieves a significant quality elevation of 0.32 (0.26-0.35) over the baseline WN model. The model's efficiency and quality make it an attractive alternative to transform-based models such as Transformer-based generative networks (TFGN) with an implementation cost of 0.5 billion parameters. QPNET-UC offers a compelling balance of performance, efficiency, and compactness suitable for a variety of audio synthesis applications. The model's ability to manage complex spectral contents using a simple yet effective layer also provides a valuable reference for the development of future neural audio synthesis models. The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we investigate how impulsive behavior affects decision
making, which yields interesting insights into the Tsallis delay discounting model.
We also demonstrate that our model offers a clearer distinction between time
discounting and impulsivity, which are separately captured, and that time
discounting's influence can be regulated through a constant factor, whereas
impulsivity's impact is more complex and dependent on the model's standard
deviation. Additionally, we investigate how our model's predictions align with
existing datasets, which reveals surprising results indicating that delay discounting
models may overestimate the time discounting effect, and that our model's more
gradual decrease in benefits over time is consistent with consumers' actual behavior
in wait experiments. We also explore the possibility that delay discounting's
increase in the time discounting effect over time may be an experimental artifact
resulting from participants' growing awareness of the experiment's true time frames.
Lastly, we examine the implications of our model for the economics literature and
identify key areas for further research. We conclude that delay discounting models
can be a powerful tool for capturing time discounting's complex nature, and that
our model provides a useful framework for exploring the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. However, we also acknowledge the limitations of our study, which
only focuses on the Tsallis delay discounting model's implications, and fail to
address critical issues such as the model's estimation, as well as the choice of the

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating multiple factors that influence water content, including temperature, redox conditions, and temperature-duration of thermal metamorphism, we established that temperature had the most significant effect on the observed water content. Nevertheless, even when factoring in temperature, the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals still exhibited water contents that were 3-16 times lower than those found in the Antarctic samples. Previous research identified a similar D-poor isotopic signature in metal components from the Chelyabinsk fall, suggesting an independent line of evidence. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$ for the XXZ chain, confirming that correlation functions of the model can be represented through vertex operators of the algebra. This representation enables us to derive closed formulas for one-point form factors. Additionally, we identify a direct relationship between the F-basis of the algebra and the Bethe roots. This connection allows us to determine the leading and next-to-leading order terms in the algebra's norm-square, as a function of both spin and Bethe parameters. Furthermore, we establish that the algebra's central extension is relevant to its representation, and demonstrate the association of its primary fields with single-Bethe-root states. Lastly, we present a possible approach to generalizing our findings to other integrable models. This includes the XYZ chain and the t-J chain, for which some key algebraic and statistical-mixture criteria can be met. However, further investigation is required to fully determine their representations of the affine quantum group. This knowledge could ultimately be utilized to compute the correlation functions of these models. In the case of the XXZ chain, we have already derived the closed formulas, leveraging its representation of the affine quantum group. This achievement is significant, as it resolves a long-standing issue in theoretical physics. This concern revolved around the query of whether it is possible to achieve a comprehensive, systematic, and consistent understanding of the physical properties of quantum systems, solely through the utilization of quantum-group symmetry. Our study provides a resounding affirmation of this possibility. Speech-to-text translation, a highly sought-after language tool, has multiple applications but has not yet been fully incorporated into everyday use due to the limited number of language pairs it supports. One significant hurdle in expanding this technology is the need for extensive parallel data to train translation models, a challenge that has not been fully addressed despite advancements in machine learning. This paper introduces a novel approach, called Zero-shot Speech-to-text, that enables the translation of speech into a target language without any training on the specific language pair. This innovative technique uses a common intermediate language, known as a hub language, to facilitate translations between any two languages in which the models are trained. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating a small amount of parallel data in the target language significantly improves the translation quality, with the best results achieved when the intermediate language is the same as the speech input language. Our model also excels in comparison to models trained on parallel data for certain language pairs. Notably, it surpasses the state-of-the-art system trained on parallel data for the Spanish-English task and matches the quality of a system trained on parallel data for the English-French task. Our analysis reveals that speech-to-text translation models inherit the speech-to-speech translation's ability to translate without training on each individual language pair, albeit with a lower level of ability. It is interesting to note that English is an exceptionally easy hub language to use, likely because it has a vast amount of resources available which could positively impact the model's performance. Our analysis also indicates that selecting the most linguistically similar hub language yields the best results, with a notable example being the selection of French as the hub language for translating English into French. Our analysis also provides an initial insight into zero-shot speech-to-text through the lens of multi-layered linear classification. Our study is an initial exploration into zero-shot speech-to-text, and there are numerous aspects that merit further research, including the integration of pre-trained models, the utilization of additional data, and the evaluation of speech-to-text translation in comparison to speech-speech translation. Our study's findings warrant a deeper examination of the relationships between speech, speech-to-text, and speech-to-speech translation, as well as a better comprehension of the linear classification's role in zero-shot speech-to-text. Our study's results encourage a more in-depth analysis of the role of hub languages in zero-shot speech-to-text, with a focus on the impact of selecting a particular hub language rather than another. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain changes in variational geometry. Specifically, if two geometric setups are closely related, or 'birational', we can derive how the related quantum cohomology system appears and functions within this new setup of geometry. This understanding allows us to identify a specific'mirror symmetry' effect that occurs when the geometry is modified in a way that reflects changes in the original geometry. This research also demonstrates that when the geometry is modified in a more complex way that includes multiple reflections, the related quantum cohomology system will exhibit a 'Fock space' structure, reminiscent of an abstract mathematical concept. This work expands our knowledge of quantum cohomology and its connection to'mirror symmetry', a fundamental idea in this field of research. This study was conducted by teams of researchers led by R. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is designed for various
users, from laboratory personnel to industry professionals, research scientists,
and academic staff, providing a straightforward and user-friendly interface
for both fundamental and applied applications. ViDaExpert is an enhanced version
of ViDa, previously introduced in [1], with novel features including an
intuitive graphical interface, a more efficient algorithm for K-Means, the ability
to add custom shaders for visualizations, and a new interface for feature
selection, among other improvements. The application is available for download
at [2]. ViDaExpert is the result of the research outlined in [3]. The developer
of ViDaExpert, J. M. Serradillo, is currently seeking new collaborations and
projects to continue developing the software. The developer can be reached at
jmserradillo@unicauca.edu. The application is distributed under the terms of the
GPL3. ViDaExpert is developed using C++ and Qt, with 3D graphics handled by
VistaGL. The application is compatible with Unix-like operating systems and
Windows 10. The developer of ViDaExpert would like to acknowledge the support
provided by COLCIENCIAS (CIOER-0019-2017) and the University of Cauca. ViDaExpert
is capable of handling large datasets; however, its performance may be impacted

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. In the process, we develop an implicit time-stepping method for an heat equation that includes a Newtonian volume integral, which further highlights the efficiency of our new method. Our code is openly accessible for review and use. In addition, we address the challenge of computing complex logarithmic integrals arising from certain volume potentials by transforming them into boundary integrals and using our method, which results in a significant improvement in efficiency. This modification enables us to solve a specific volume-integral heat equation problem more efficiently. Our new method can be applied to multiple domain configurations, including overlapping domains. However, resolving singularities that arise when points on the boundary are close to the intersection of two edges requires further investigation. In this paper, we propose a new approach based on an edge-based decomposition, which provides a more stable framework for addressing such singularities. This revised approach ensures that the boundary values of the potential become more accurate, especially close to the intersection of two edges. We have successfully applied our new method to multiple test cases, including those involving non-smooth functions and physical models that produce singularities. Our results prove that our new algorithm delivers highly accurate and stable outcomes.
